Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: Hantavirus RNA Detection in Small Mammals and Spatial Comparison with Reported Human HFRS Cases in West Kazakhstan Region, 2025
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic disease associated with orthohantaviruses maintained in natural rodent hosts. This study assessed the detection and spatial distribution of hantavirus RNA among small mammals in the West Kazakhstan Region in 2025 and compared rodent surveillance findings with human HFRS occurrence. An observational cross-sectional analytical study was conducted in July and September 2025 in four districts. A total of 343 small mammals were captured and morphologically identified. Lung tissue samples from 329 animals collected in September were examined in 123 pooled testing units, whereas 14 animals collected in July were tested individually. Thus, 137 testing units representing 343 animals were evaluated by real-time and conventional RT-PCR. The minimum infection rate (MIR) was calculated as a descriptive minimum estimate, and a pooled-testing likelihood model was used to account for variation in testing-unit size. Hantavirus RNA was detected in 47/137 testing units, including 45 positive pooled units and two individually positive specimens. Based on 343 individual animals, the descriptive MIR was 13.7%. The model-based individual-level infection probability was estimated at 18.0% (95% profile-likelihood CI: 13.5–23.1%). Positive testing units were observed among the Ural field mouse (Apodemus uralensis), bank vole (Myodes glareolus), and common vole (Microtus arvalis). At the district level, the descriptive MIR ranged from 11.6% in Burlinsky to 19.0% in Chingirlauisky. Sampling sites overlapped spatially with settlements reporting human HFRS cases, including Utvinka, Daryinsk, and Rubezhinskoye; however, spatial coincidence does not establish direct transmission.

An observational cross-sectional analytical study was conducted in July and September 2025 in four districts. A total of 343 small mammals were captured and morphologically identified. Lung tissue samples from 329 animals collected in September were examined in 123 pooled testing units, whereas 14 animals collected in July were tested individually. Thus, 137 testing units representing 343 animals were evaluated by real-time and conventional RT-PCR. The minimum infection rate (MIR) was calculated as a descriptive minimum estimate, and a pooled-testing likelihood model was used to account for variation in testing-unit size. Hantavirus RNA was detected in 47/137 testing units, including 45 positive pooled units and two individually positive specimens. Based on 343 individual animals, the descriptive MIR was 13.7%. The model-based individual-level infection probability was estimated at 18.0% (95% profile-likelihood CI: 13.5–23.1%). Positive testing units were observed among the Ural field mouse (Apodemus uralensis), bank vole (Myodes glareolus), and common vole (Microtus arvalis). At the district level, the descriptive MIR ranged from 11.6% in Burlinsky to 19.0% in Chingirlauisky. Sampling sites overlapped spatially with settlements reporting human HFRS cases, including Utvinka, Daryinsk, and Rubezhinskoye; however, spatial coincidence does not establish direct transmission.

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热(肾综合征出血热)是一种人畜共患疾病,与在自然啮齿动物宿主中维持的正汉坦病毒有关。

papers.title: Structural basis for protocadherin-1 recognition by New World hantaviruses
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are rodent-borne pathogens that cause severe human disease for which no approved therapeutics are available. New World hantaviruses, including Andes virus (ANDV), use the cell-surface receptor protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) to enter host cells1. However, the structural basis of this interaction remains unclear. Here we describe the structure of PCDH1 bound to the ANDV spike at near-atomic resolution. PCDH1 asymmetrically engages a deep central pocket formed by four Gn protomers in the spike, explaining why only intact viral particles or soluble tetramers recognize it. Mutagenesis identified three Gn loops that shape the receptor-binding site and afford the transfer of PCDH1 binding from New World to Old World glycoproteins. Structural and functional analyses of four neutralizing antibodies revealed that they block receptor binding through two distinct mechanisms—occluding access to the PCDH1-binding site or sterically preventing receptor engagement. Together, these findings define the structural determinants of hantavirus–receptor recognition, reveal how a virus can mask its receptor-binding site by recessing it in a surface depression and how antibodies can counter this strategy, and provide a framework for the design of antiviral therapeutics targeting the hantavirus spike. The structure of PCDH1 bound to the ANDV spike defines the structural determinants of hantavirus–receptor recognition.

papers.title_zh: 新世界 汉坦病毒 病毒对 protocadherin-1 识别的结构基础

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒 病毒是啮齿动物传播的病原体,可导致严重的人类疾病,且缺乏获批的治疗药物 (A1);新世界的 汉坦病毒 病毒,如 安第斯病毒,利用细胞表面受体 protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) 进入宿主细胞 (A2)。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者解析了 PCDH1 与 ANDV 蛋白棘突结合的近原子分辨率结构 (A4),通过 Gn 环的突变分析确定了受体结合特征 (A6),并对四种中和抗体进行结构和功能分析,以评估阻断机制 (A7)。
analysis_zh.results: PCDH1 不对称地结合由四个 Gn 蛋白亚基形成的深部中心口袋 (A5);三个 Gn 环塑造结合位点并使 PCDH1 的结合能够转移至旧世界糖蛋白 (A6);抗体通过遮挡位点或空间位阻阻止受体结合,从而实现阻断 (A7);总体而言,该结构阐明了 汉坦病毒‐受体识别的决定因素 (A4,A8,A9)。

papers.title: Risk Communication in a Post-Pandemic World: Lessons from the 2026 Andes Virus Outbreak
papers.abstract: In May 2026, a hantavirus outbreak aboard the MV Hondius cruise ship triggered public alarm disproportionate to its actual scale, despite the rapid diagnosis, clear WHO and ECDC guidance, and swift containment within three months. This commentary asks why outbreaks that health authorities handle correctly can still produce pandemic-level panic. Drawing on media framing research and the Hondius case itself, there seem to be two forces at work. One is news coverage that foregrounds alarming questions while burying expert reassurances. The second one is that post-pandemic public has learnt to distrust reassurance after Covid, when authorities failed to convey that guidance would evolve. This piece contends that clear, accurate and timely statements from health authorities are no longer sufficient on their own and proposes three practices going forward. Recommendations involve naming and directly addressing alarming narratives early, treating community trust as infrastructure built before a crisis rather than during one, and engaging with social media conversations directly rather than relying solely on content removal. Since it was small and well controlled, this outbreak offers a low-cost opportunity to test these practices before a larger outbreak makes the same communication gap far more costly.

analysis.background: The May 2026 Andes hantavirus outbreak on the MV Hondius sparked public alarm far exceeding its limited scale despite rapid diagnosis, clear WHO/ECDC guidance, and swift containment. This commentary asks why well‑managed outbreaks still generate pandemic‑level panic.
analysis.main_directions: The author identifies two driving forces: media framing that highlights alarming questions while downplaying expert reassurance, and a post‑COVID public distrust of official reassurances.
analysis.current_state: Current evidence suggests that clear, accurate, and timely statements from health authorities alone no longer suffice to prevent panic.
analysis.gaps: The gap lies in the failure of news coverage to balance alarmist narratives with expert input and the lingering distrust cultivated during the COVID‑19 pandemic.
analysis.future_research: The piece proposes three practices—early naming of alarming narratives, building community trust as pre‑crisis infrastructure, and direct engagement with social‑media conversations—and recommends testing them in the controlled Hondius outbreak as a low‑cost pilot.

analysis.summary_en: Background: The May 2026 Andes hantavirus outbreak on the MV Hondius caused disproportionate alarm despite rapid, expert‑led containment, prompting a review of why such events still incite panic. Main directions: Two forces drive this—media framing that amplifies fear and post‑COVID distrust of official reassurance. Current state: Clear, timely authority statements alone are now insufficient to curb panic. Gaps: News coverage often neglects expert reassurance, and public trust remains eroded from the COVID era. Future research: Test three proposed practices—early narrative naming, pre‑crisis trust building, and direct social‑media engagement—using the Hondius outbreak as a low‑cost pilot.

analysis_zh.background: 2026年5月,MV Hondius上的安第斯病毒汉坦病毒爆发引发公众恐慌,远超其有限规模,尽管诊断迅速、世卫组织/欧盟疾病预防控制中心提供了明确指导并迅速控制。本文探讨为何管理良好的疫情仍会产生类似大流行的恐慌。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 作者指出两大驱动力:媒体框架强调令人担忧的问题而淡化专家安抚,以及疫情后公众对官方安抚的持续不信任。
analysis_zh.current_state: 目前证据表明,单靠卫生部门的清晰、准确、及时声明已不足以防止恐慌。
analysis_zh.gaps: 差距在于新闻报道未能平衡惊悚叙事与专家意见,以及COVID‐19疫情期间形成的持续不信任。
analysis_zh.future_research: 本文提出三项实践——提前命名令人担忧的叙事、将社区信任作为危机前基础设施,以及直接参与社交媒体对话——并建议在受控的Hondius爆发中以低成本试点进行测试。

papers.full_text: Can Hantavirus cruise into the next pandemic? Despite concerns arising from a recent ship-associated outbreak on the M/V Hondius cruise, current evidence suggests that Andes virus (ANDV) poses a low pandemic risk. Nevertheless, viral evolution, ecological changes, and reservoir host dynamics could drive future emergence of ANDV, underscoring the need for improved surveillance, diagnostics, therapeutics, and vaccine preparedness. Hantaviruses are part of the family Hantaviridae, which comprises eight genera. Among them, viruses associated with human disease belong to the genus Orthohantavirus. Orthohantaviruses are enveloped, tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA viruses whose genome consists of small (S), medium (M), and large (L) segments encoding the nucleocapsid protein (N), glycoproteins Gn/Gc, and the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), respectively. The two major clinical diseases caused by orthohantaviruses are haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome/cardiopulmonary syndrome (HPS/HCPS). HFRS is mainly caused by Asian and European orthohantaviruses, including Hantaan virus, Seoul virus, Puumala virus, and Dobrava virus, and primarily affects the kidneys. In contrast, HPS/HCPS is caused by several American orthohantaviruses, including Orthohantavirus sinnonbrenense (Sin Nombre virus; SNV) and Orthohantavirus andesense (Andes virus; ANDV), and is characterised by severe respiratory disease, pulmonary oedema, and cardiovascular compromise. Importantly, ANDV-associated HPS is characterised by high case-fatality rates, with mortality estimates in Chile and Argentina ranging from approximately 21% to 50%. Orthohantavirus infection is primarily acquired by inhaling aerosolised particles contaminated with the urine, saliva, or faeces of infected rodents, although transmission may also occur through direct contact with contaminated materials or rodent bites. While most orthohantaviruses are transmitted exclusively from rodents to humans, ANDV is unique among orthohantaviruses for its demonstrated capacity for person-to-person transmission, particularly during close, prolonged contact with symptomatic individuals. Although sustained community transmission has not been demonstrated, ANDV remains the only orthohantavirus for which person-to-person transmission has been consistently documented, predominantly among close household or intimate contacts. On 4 May 2026, an international cluster of ANDV infections was identified among passengers travelling aboard the M/V Hondius following its departure from Ushuaia, Argentina. The event prompted a multinational public health response involving case isolation, quarantine, surveillance, contact tracing, and genomic investigation. The WHO declared the outbreak over on 2 July 2026, with 13 cases reported, including 3 fatalities. The M/V Hondius cluster therefore provides an important contemporary example of ANDV’s epidemic potential. Could ANDV cause a future pandemic? Despite documented person-to-person transmission associated with the M/V Hondius cluster, current epidemiological and genomic evidence indicates that the likelihood of this outbreak progressing to sustained epidemic or pandemic transmission was exceedingly low. Prompt implementation of public health interventions, including quarantine measures and active surveillance of individuals aboard the vessel, facilitated the early identification and isolation of suspected cases. Furthermore, genomic analyses revealed remarkably limited viral diversity among sequenced cases from the M/V Hondius cluster, with identical S and M segment sequences and only two synonymous single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) detected within the L segment, one in case 5 and another in case 7. Importantly, no evidence of amino acid changes associated with enhanced transmissibility or sustained human-to-human spread was identified. In contrast, the outbreak sequences showed approximately 98.7% nucleotide identity across all three genome segments with ANDV sequences identified in Argentina in 1997 and 2018, indicating considerably greater divergence from these historical reference sequences. Furthermore, the reported positive cases fell within the incubation period of nine to 45 days for ANDV, suggesting that the cluster may have originated from a limited zoonotic exposure event, potentially followed by restricted secondary transmission, and is unlikely to develop into an epidemic or a pandemic event. However, given that ANDV has historically caused multiple outbreaks, it is important to highlight the conditions that could enable localised ANDV outbreaks to evolve and escalate into larger epidemics, and potentially, under exceptional circumstances, into a pandemic threat among human populations, as illustrated in Figure. Potential drivers of Andes virus (ANDV) outbreak escalation and pandemic emergence. ANDV is maintained in rodent reservoirs, primarily the long-tailed pygmy rice rat (Oligoryzomys longicaudatus), and is transmitted to humans through inhalation of aerosolised rodent excreta. Unlike other orthohantaviruses, ANDV can also undergo limited person-to-person transmission, although sustained community transmission has not been documented. The graphical abstract highlights three factors that could contribute to outbreak escalation: (i) viral evolution through mutation, reassortment, and host adaptation; (ii) environmental and ecological changes that increase rodent abundance and spillover risk; and (iii) expansion of reservoir host range through host switching and reservoir diversification. Under favourable ecological and evolutionary conditions, these processes could increase the scale, frequency, geographic distribution, or transmission potential of future outbreaks, underscoring the importance of continued surveillance, preparedness, and the development of effective diagnostics, therapeutics, and vaccines. Illustration created with BioRender.com. First - The acquisition of beneficial mutations may facilitate adaptation to human hosts. Genetic variation arising during viral replication could theoretically influence viral fitness, host range, or transmission efficiency under selective pressures. Orthohantaviruses replicate using an error-prone RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), with evolutionary rates estimated at approximately 10−2-10−4 substitutions per site per year, consistent with rates reported for other RNA viruses. However, the relationship between genomic variation and altered transmissibility in ANDV remains incompletely understood, and no specific adaptive mutations have yet been conclusively associated with sustained human-to-human transmission. Previous studies have shown that ANDV strains from rodent and human hosts can produce markedly different outcomes in the Syrian hamster model. Notably, a Chilean human isolate (CHI-7913), recovered from a fatal HPS case, acquired only a single non-synonymous mutation after 25 serial passages in hamsters and remained non-pathogenic, indicating relative genomic stability. In contrast, the rodent-derived isolate Chile-9717869 causes uniformly lethal disease despite differing by 23 amino acids from CHI-7913. Although these findings suggest a degree of genomic stability, they do not necessarily preclude adaptation. One possible explanation is that the CHI-7913 isolate had already undergone host-specific adaptation following zoonotic transmission to humans, thereby enhancing fitness in human cells while reducing replication efficiency and pathogenicity in the Syrian hamster model. Collectively, these observations indicate that relatively few genetic changes can substantially alter host adaptation and disease phenotype in ANDV, while the molecular determinants governing virulence and transmissibility remain incompletely understood. Several biological mechanisms may contribute to these processes, including alterations in receptor usage, interferon antagonism, and genome reassortment. Pathogenic orthohantaviruses utilise β3 integrins, protocadherin-1, and other endothelium-associated receptors for host-cell entry, and mutations affecting glycoprotein-receptor interactions could alter host permissiveness and enhance adaptation to humans. In addition, the ability of orthohantaviruses to suppress interferon signalling contributes to reservoir persistence and may influence pathogenicity across different hosts. Importantly, the segmented orthohantavirus genome permits genetic reassortment during co-infection, potentially generating novel phenotypic combinations with altered virulence, transmissibility, or host range. Although reassortment appears less frequent than in other members of the order Bunyavirales (e.g. orthobunyaviruses) and influenza viruses, it remains an important mechanism contributing to long-term evolutionary adaptation and host expansion. Second - An increase in rodent reservoir populations driven by environmental and ecological changes may amplify the risk of zoonotic spillover. Environmental disruption is a well-recognised determinant of orthohantavirus emergence and transmission dynamics. Climatic oscillations, including El Niño-associated rainfall patterns, can substantially increase rodent abundance and population density, thereby elevating opportunities for human exposure, as previously documented during Sin Nombre virus (SNV) outbreaks in North America. In South America, deforestation, agricultural expansion, urban encroachment into rural and forested ecosystems, and biodiversity disturbance may similarly intensify contact between humans and ANDV reservoir hosts. In parallel, globalisation and expanding transportation networks have facilitated the international dissemination of rodent-associated orthohantaviruses, as illustrated by the spread of Seoul virus (SEOV) through maritime trade and the pet rat industry. Collectively, these ecological and anthropogenic pressures may increase the frequency of spillover events and the geographic distribution of orthohantavirus exposure. However, there is currently no evidence that such conditions alone are sufficient to drive sustained human-to-human transmission or pandemic-level spread of ANDV. Third - Expansion of reservoir host range may contribute to broader geographic dissemination and increased opportunities for human exposure. Orthohantaviruses were historically considered highly host-specific pathogens, with individual virus lineages predominantly associated with a single rodent reservoir species through long-term co-evolutionary relationships. ANDV is primarily associated with Oligoryzomys longicaudatus as its principal reservoir host. However, accumulating phylogenetic and ecological evidence has challenged the concept of strict host specificity, demonstrating that host-switching events, spillover infections, and reservoir diversification have likely occurred repeatedly throughout orthohantavirus evolutionary history. In addition, the identification of genetically divergent orthohantaviruses in shrews, moles, and bats suggests that ancestral orthohantaviruses may have undergone multiple historical cross-species transmission events. Collectively, these findings indicate that orthohantavirus host associations, although generally stable, are not biologically absolute. Habitat disruptions, altered species interactions, and environmental pressures could therefore increase opportunities for cross-species transmission and geographic expansion over extended ecological timescales, potentially increasing the frequency of human exposure to infected reservoir hosts. Nevertheless, there is currently no evidence that such ecological processes have resulted in ANDV lineages with enhanced sustained human-to-human transmissibility. Current preparedness against ANDV outbreaks Perhaps more worrying is the limited availability of rapid diagnostics, antivirals, and vaccines for responding to outbreaks of ANDV and other clinically relevant orthohantaviruses. Several antiviral and immunotherapeutic strategies have been explored against human disease-causing orthohantaviruses, including nucleoside analogues such as ribavirin, favipiravir and ETAR; entry inhibitors such as lactoferrin and griffithsin; host-directed approaches targeting vascular leakage pathways; RNAi-based strategies; and, more recently, neutralising monoclonal antibodies targeting the Gn/Gc glycoprotein complex. However, no orthohantavirus-specific antiviral has yet become an established standard of care, and most candidates remain experimental or dependent on very early administration. In parallel, vaccine development efforts have advanced substantially over the past decades. Hantavax®, an inactivated orthohantavirus vaccine marketed in South Korea to prevent HFRS caused by Hantaan and Seoul viruses, remains among the only orthohantavirus vaccines licensed for human use, while several next-generation vaccine candidates are currently under development and evaluation in preclinical and early-phase clinical trials. Despite these advances, effective countermeasures specifically targeting ANDV remain limited, highlighting an important preparedness gap for future outbreaks. In conclusion - Overall, current evidence does not support the conclusion that ANDV is imminently poised to emerge as a pandemic pathogen comparable to severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). Nevertheless, under favourable ecological and epidemiological conditions, localised ANDV outbreaks may increase in scale or geographic distribution, potentially posing broader regional public health challenges. These considerations underscore the importance of strengthening preparedness strategies to prevent the escalation of orthohantavirus outbreaks, particularly in under-resourced endemic regions of South America. Integrated ecological surveillance approaches, including climate-informed forecasting of rodent population dynamics, together with genomic epidemiological surveillance of ANDV and other clinically relevant orthohantaviruses, may improve early detection of spillover risk, characterise orthohantavirus diversity and evolutionary dynamics, and support timely public health responses. In addition, expanded availability of antiviral therapeutics, monoclonal antibodies, preventive vaccines, and rapid diagnostic platforms will be important for comprehensive orthohantavirus outbreak preparedness and response. These diagnostic platforms could include lateral-flow assays to detect orthohantavirus-specific IgM and IgG antibodies in symptomatic patients, as well as antigen-based tests for direct virus detection in both humans and reservoir hosts. full_text_sections.full_text: Can Hantavirus cruise into the next pandemic? Despite concerns arising from a recent ship-associated outbreak on the M/V Hondius cruise, current evidence suggests that Andes virus (ANDV) poses a low pandemic risk. Nevertheless, viral evolution, ecological changes, and reservoir host dynamics could drive future emergence of ANDV, underscoring the need for improved surveillance, diagnostics, therapeutics, and vaccine preparedness. Hantaviruses are part of the family Hantaviridae, which comprises eight genera. Among them, viruses associated with human disease belong to the genus Orthohantavirus. Orthohantaviruses are enveloped, tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA viruses whose genome consists of small (S), medium (M), and large (L) segments encoding the nucleocapsid protein (N), glycoproteins Gn/Gc, and the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), respectively. The two major clinical diseases caused by orthohantaviruses are haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome/cardiopulmonary syndrome (HPS/HCPS). HFRS is mainly caused by Asian and European orthohantaviruses, including Hantaan virus, Seoul virus, Puumala virus, and Dobrava virus, and primarily affects the kidneys. In contrast, HPS/HCPS is caused by several American orthohantaviruses, including Orthohantavirus sinnonbrenense (Sin Nombre virus; SNV) and Orthohantavirus andesense (Andes virus; ANDV), and is characterised by severe respiratory disease, pulmonary oedema, and cardiovascular compromise. Importantly, ANDV-associated HPS is characterised by high case-fatality rates, with mortality estimates in Chile and Argentina ranging from approximately 21% to 50%. Orthohantavirus infection is primarily acquired by inhaling aerosolised particles contaminated with the urine, saliva, or faeces of infected rodents, although transmission may also occur through direct contact with contaminated materials or rodent bites. While most orthohantaviruses are transmitted exclusively from rodents to humans, ANDV is unique among orthohantaviruses for its demonstrated capacity for person-to-person transmission, particularly during close, prolonged contact with symptomatic individuals. Although sustained community transmission has not been demonstrated, ANDV remains the only orthohantavirus for which person-to-person transmission has been consistently documented, predominantly among close household or intimate contacts. On 4 May 2026, an international cluster of ANDV infections was identified among passengers travelling aboard the M/V Hondius following its departure from Ushuaia, Argentina. The event prompted a multinational public health response involving case isolation, quarantine, surveillance, contact tracing, and genomic investigation. The WHO declared the outbreak over on 2 July 2026, with 13 cases reported, including 3 fatalities. Furthermore, the reported positive cases fell within the incubation period of nine to 45 days for ANDV, suggesting that the cluster may have originated from a limited zoonotic exposure event, potentially followed by restricted secondary transmission, and is unlikely to develop into an epidemic or a pandemic event. papers.title: Hantaviruses as Emerging Zoonotic Pathogens: Molecular Biology, Epidemiology, Therapeutics, vaccine, and Pathogenesis.
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are globally distributed zoonotic pathogens belonging to the family Hantaviridae and are responsible for two major human diseases, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS). Despite substantial progress in hantavirus research, important challenges remain in understanding the interactions among viral evolution, reservoir ecology, environmental change, transmission dynamics, and host immunopathology. This review provides an integrated One Health perspective that connects molecular virology and host-virus interactions with transmission ecology, global epidemiology, and the mechanisms underlying vascular leakage and severe disease. In addition to summarizing established knowledge, we highlight recent advances in hantavirus taxonomy, genomic and molecular surveillance, ecological and transmission modeling, and the identification of hantavirus circulation in previously underrecognized regions. Particular emphasis is placed on the role of reservoir host dynamics, climate and environmental change, habitat disturbance, and human-wildlife interactions in shaping spillover risk, as well as on endothelial dysfunction, immune dysregulation, and coagulation abnormalities as interconnected mechanisms of disease severity. We also identify persistent knowledge gaps concerning host susceptibility, viral persistence, determinants of differential virulence and tissue tropism, interspecies transmission, and the development of effective antiviral therapies and vaccines. By integrating these complementary perspectives, this review provides a framework for understanding hantavirus emergence and pathogenesis while identifying priorities for future surveillance, prevention, and therapeutic research.

Despite substantial progress in hantavirus research, important challenges remain in understanding the interactions among viral evolution, reservoir ecology, environmental change, transmission dynamics, and host immunopathology. This review provides an integrated One Health perspective that connects molecular virology and host-virus interactions with transmission ecology, global epidemiology, and the mechanisms underlying vascular leakage and severe disease. In addition to summarizing established knowledge, we highlight recent advances in hantavirus taxonomy, genomic and molecular surveillance, ecological and transmission modeling, and the identification of hantavirus circulation in previously underrecognized regions. Particular emphasis is placed on the role of reservoir host dynamics, climate and environmental change, habitat disturbance, and human-wildlife interactions in shaping spillover risk, as well as on endothelial dysfunction, immune dysregulation, and coagulation abnormalities as interconnected mechanisms of disease severity. We also identify persistent knowledge gaps concerning host susceptibility, viral persistence, determinants of differential virulence and tissue tropism, interspecies transmission, and the development of effective antiviral therapies and vaccines. By integrating these complementary perspectives, this review provides a framework for understanding hantavirus emergence and pathogenesis while identifying priorities for future surveillance, prevention, and therapeutic research.

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒es 作为新兴的动物源性病原体:分子生物学、流行病学、治疗学、疫苗及发病机制。

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒es 是全球分布的动物源性病原体,可导致 肾综合征出血热(HFRS)和 汉坦病毒心肺综合征(HCPS)。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述强调了将病毒进化、储备宿主生态、环境变化、传播动力学以及宿主免疫病理学联系起来的挑战。
analysis_zh.current_state: 它提出了一个 One Health 框架,整合了分子病毒学、宿主‐病毒相互作用、传播生态、全球流行病学以及血管渗漏和重症机制。
analysis_zh.gaps: 持续存在的空白包括宿主易感性、病毒持久性、致病性和组织嗜性的决定因素、跨种传播,以及缺乏有效的抗病毒药物或疫苗。
analysis_zh.future_research: 优先事项是加强监测、生态与传播建模、储备宿主动态及气候影响的研究,以及抗病毒疗法和疫苗的开发。

papers.summary_zh: 背景：汉坦病毒es 是全球分布的动物源性病原体,可导致 肾综合征出血热(HFRS)和 汉坦病毒心肺综合征(HCPS)。 主要方向：本综述强调了将病毒进化、储备宿主生态、环境变化、传播动力学以及宿主免疫病理学联系起来的挑战。 研究现状：它提出了一个 One Health 框架,整合了分子病毒学、宿主‐病毒相互作用、传播生态、全球流行病学以及血管渗漏和重症机制。 不足：持续存在的空白包括宿主易感性、病毒持久性、致病性和组织嗜性的决定因素、跨种传播,以及缺乏有效的抗病毒药物或疫苗。 后续研究：优先事项是加强监测、生态与传播建模、储备宿主动态及气候影响的研究,以及抗病毒疗法和疫苗的开发。

papers.title: Expanded protocadherin-1 usage reveals a broader hantavirus entry landscape.
papers.abstract: Mammalian hantaviruses are RNA viruses that cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in the Americas and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Eurasia. The cellular entry mechanisms of most hantaviruses remain poorly defined. To examine entry by phylogenetically distinct hantaviruses identified across Africa, Eurasia, and the Americas, we generated replication-competent recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses (rVSVs) bearing Gn/Gc proteins from Necoclí, Sangassou, Thottapalayam, Kenkeme, Nova, Oxbow, and Tula viruses. All these Gn/Gc proteins except Kenkeme supported infection of primary human endothelial cells, indicating that endothelial cell entry is permissive for a broader range of hantaviruses than previously appreciated. Except for rVSV-Kenkeme, these rVSVs did not acquire additional mutations beyond pre-engineered rescue-enhancing changes during rescue and passaging. Genetic studies in human cells lacking protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) showed that Necoclí, Tula, and Nova viruses use PCDH1 for efficient infection, although the Nova phenotype was weaker. These three Gn/Gc proteins bound soluble PCDH1 with different apparent avidities, and infection by the corresponding rVSVs was inhibited by soluble PCDH1; Necoclí and Tula, but not Nova, were also blocked by a PCDH1-targeting monoclonal antibody. Authentic Tula virus infection was similarly reduced in PCDH1 knockout endothelial cells. Finally, the broadly reactive anti-Gn/Gc human monoclonal antibody ADI-42898 efficiently neutralized Necoclí, Nova, Sangassou, and Kenkeme rVSVs, but showed weak or undetectable activity against Oxbow, Tula, and Thottapalayam rVSVs. Together, these findings expand the range of hantavirus glycoproteins capable of mediating infection of human endothelial cells, broaden the phylogenetic scope of PCDH1-dependent entry, and identify receptor-targeted and viral glycoprotein-targeted strategies with differential activity.IMPORTANCEMany newly discovered hantaviruses are known only from sequence data, leaving their ability to enter human cells and their receptor usage unresolved. Using a BSL2-compatible recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus (rVSV) system, we show that glycoproteins from several divergent hantaviruses can mediate infection of primary human endothelial cells, indicating that endothelial cell entry is permissive for a broader range of hantaviruses than previously appreciated. We also show that protocadherin-1 (PCDH1), previously linked mainly to New World hantaviruses, is used by Necoclí, Tula, and Nova viruses but not universally across the panel, revealing broader but heterogeneous receptor usage. An authentic Tula virus experiment supports this conclusion beyond the surrogate system. Finally, a broadly reactive anti-Gn/Gc antibody neutralizes several, but not all, of these viruses, highlighting both the promise and the limits of broadly protective countermeasures and the utility of these rVSVs for evaluating entry inhibitors.

When humans are accidentally exposed to 63 aerosolized excreta from infected reservoir hosts, rodent-borne hantaviruses can cause 64 severe, often fatal diseases, such as hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) in 65 the Americas and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Europe and Asia(2, 66 3). Periodic hantavirus outbreaks continue to occur, and Andes virus (ANDV) is notable 67 for rare human-to-human transmission in a close-contact setting, such as on the MV 68 Hondius Cruise Ship in April-May 2026(4–7). Despite their significant impact on public 69 health, there are currently no FDA-approved vaccines or therapeutics for hantavirus 70 infections, and our understanding of their entry mechanisms remains poor(2, 8). 71 Studies based on genetic sequencing over the past few decades have discovered 72 many new mammalian hantaviruses carried by rodents, insectivores, and bats(9, 10). 73 Currently, the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV) recognizes 48 74 species of mammalian hantaviruses globally(11). However, for most of these 75 hantaviruses, no virus isolates are available, and their potential to cause human infection 76 and illness remains unknown(12). Additionally, the need for high-level biocontainment 77 (BSL3) in hantavirus research and the lack of a robust reverse genetics systems to study 78 the complete hantavirus infection cycle greatly hinder our understanding of their 79 biology(2). 80 Hantavirus particles carry a negative-sense, tripartite genome composed of small 81 (S), medium (M), and large (L) segments(13). The S segment encodes the nucleoprotein 82 (N), which coats the genome; the L segment encodes the L protein, which possesses 83 Page 5 of 40 RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and endoribonuclease activities required for genome 84 replication and transcription, respectively. The M segment encodes the glycoprotein 85 complex as a single polyprotein, which is processed by cellular proteases to generate the 86 Gn and Gc glycoproteins(14). The Gn/Gc heterodimers are arranged in a tetrameric 87 cloverleaf-like structure on hantavirus particles, forming spikes(15). Gn is believed to 88 interact with host receptors, while Gc mediates fusion of the viral and endosomal 89 membranes during cellular entry(2, 15). Because Gn/Gc are necessary and sufficient to 90 mediate cellular entry, vesicular stomatitis viruses carrying Gn/Gc serve as powerful tools 91 for studying viral entry(2, 16). 92 Among proposed hantavirus entry receptors, only protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) has 93 compelling in vivo support; it is required for infection and pathogenesis of ANDV in Syrian 94 hamsters(17, 18). Genetic knockout and biochemical studies demonstrated that 100 protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) is required for the entry of 5 species of New World 101 hantaviruses: Andes virus, Sin Nombre virus (SNV), Prospect Hill virus, Maporal virus, 102 and Choclo virus, but not for the Old World hantaviruses such as Hantaan virus (HTNV), 103 Puumala virus, and Seoul virus(18, 25). The first extracellular cadherin (EC1) domain of 104 PCDH1 binds the Gn/Gc of New World hantaviruses, and disruption of the PCDH1:Gn/Gc 105 interaction by complete knockout or point mutations in EC1 protects Syrian hamsters 106 Page 6 of 40 against a lethal Andes virus challenge(17, 18). Moreover, soluble PCDH1 carrying the 107 EC1 domain and the EC1-specific monoclonal antibody (mAb-3305) neutralize rVSV- 108 ANDV and SNV infections(17, 18). However, the extent of PCDH1 usage by distinct 109 hantavirus lineages remains unknown. 110 To capture genetic, geographic, and reservoir-host variation, we focused on shrew- 111 borne Thottapalayam virus (TPMV) and Kenkeme virus (KKMV); mole-borne Nova virus 112 (NVAV), and Oxbow virus (OXBV); New World rodent-borne Necoclí virus (NECV); Old 113 World rodent-borne Sangassou virus (SANGV), and vole-borne Tula virus (TULV)(26). 114 Thottapalayam virus was first isolated from the Asian house shrew in India(27), and 115 Kenkeme virus was identified in the flat-skulled shrew in Russia(28). Nova virus is a highly 116 divergent mole-borne virus of the European mole and was initially detected in Hungary, 117 with high prevalence later documented in France(29, 30). Necoclí virus is principally 118 associated with Cherrie’s cane rat in Colombia(31). Sangassou virus is the first 119 indigenous African hantavirus isolate and was identified in the African wood mouse in 120 Guinea(32). Tula virus is classically associated with common voles and related arvicoline 121 hosts across Eurasia(26, 33). Among these viruses, Sangassou virus entry studies 122 implicated integrin β1 as a receptor(32), whereas Tula virus has the strongest direct 123 evidence of human relevance, with a molecularly confirmed symptomatic infection 124 reported in an immunocompetent patient(34). While serologic evidence suggests possible 125 human exposure to Thottapalayam and Sangassou viruses, the ability of Kenkeme, Nova, 126 Oxbow, and Necoclí viruses to cause human infection or disease remains unknown(35– 127 38). Although their reservoir-host associations are better established, human-cell tropism 128 and receptor usage remain poorly characterized for most of these viruses(26, 38). 129 Page 7 of 40 Together, these phylogenetically divergent hantaviruses associated with a variety of 130 reservoir hosts provide a framework to evaluate human cell-tropism and PCDH1 131 dependence across mammalian hantaviruses. 132 Here, we generated rVSVs expressing the Gn/Gc proteins of the seven genetically 133 and ecologically heterogeneous hantaviruses mentioned above to investigate their entry 134 mechanisms and host receptor usage. Finally, we demonstrated the utility of PCDH1 and Gn/Gc-targeting approaches 140 for neutralizing these viral infections. 141 Results 142 Divergent hantavirus Gn/Gc proteins mediate infection of human endothelial cells 143 Hantavirus Gn/Gc sequences are highly divergent across species, with 40-60% amino 144 acid differences between them. These viruses also express an enhanced GFP reporter (Fig. 2A, top 149 panel). 150 Because New World hantavirus glycoproteins are more compatible with plasma- 151 membrane budding, whereas Old World hantavirus glycoproteins are typically Golgi- 152 Page 8 of 40 localized, rVSVs bearing New World hantavirus Gn/Gc are generally rescued without 153 adaptive mutations(39, 40). In contrast, Old World hantaviruses, such as Hantaan virus 154 and Dobrava-Belgrade virus, require two mutations, I532K in the cytoplasmic tail of Gn, 155 and S1094L in the membrane-proximal part of the Gc ectodomain, to enhance rVSV 156 generation(16). These mutations are unlikely to directly affect receptor engagement 157 because they were previously shown to enhance rVSV infectivity primarily by altering 158 glycoprotein localization and incorporation into virions(16). Accordingly, we preemptively 159 altered the Gn/Gc sequences of Thottapalayam, Kenkeme, Nova, Oxbow, and 160 Sangassou viruses to incorporate HTNV-adaptive changes for rVSV generation (Fig. 2A, 161 bottom panel). 162 Plasmids encoding cognate rVSV genomes carrying codon-optimized Gn/Gc sequences 163 for expression in human cells were transfected into 293FT cells together with the helper 164 plasmids, and the resulting supernatants were used to infect Huh7.51 cells for viral 165 amplification and stock generation. In rVSV-Kenkeme, a G485R mutation, numbered according to the 169 glycoprotein precursor, was detected, although its significance remains unclear. 170 To compare infectivity, we normalized viral input by titrating the rVSVs on permissive 171 Huh7.5.1 cells. HPMECs were infected at an MOI of 1 and 174 fixed 24 hours later to assess eGFP-positive cells. All rVSVs except rVSV-Kenkeme 175 Page 9 of 40 infected these cells, although with varying efficiency (Fig. 2B). For quantitative analysis, 176 we evaluated infection at MOIs of 0.2, 1, and 5 at 8 hours post-infection. At an MOI of 177 0.2, only rVSV-Tula infection was evident (4.68%). At MOIs of 1 and 5, rVSV-Tula (23% 178 and 38%, respectively) and rVSV-Thottapalayam (6% and 18%, respectively) infection 179 was detectable, along with the positive controls rVSV-ANDV and rVSV-HTNV, whereas 180 the remaining viruses were not (Fig. 2C, left panel). 181 Kinetic experiments over 48 hrs at MOIs of 0.2 and 1 (Fig. 2C, middle and right panels, 182 respectively) further supported the higher infectivity of rVSV-Thottapalayam and rVSV- 183 Tula, and also revealed substantial infection by rVSV-Necoclí (18 and 36% at 12 hours, 184 respectively) and rVSV-Nova (32 and 38% at 48 hours, respectively). As with rVSV-ANDV, binding of rVSV-Necoclí to PCDH1 was dose 224 dependent, although of lower avidity (Fig. 4A, bottom panel). Binding of rVSV-Tula and 225 rVSV-Nova was weaker and was detectable only at higher virion inputs (Fig. 4B). 226 We next tested whether the EC1-specific mAb-3305 could block this interaction. 227 Preincubation of sEC1-2-coated plates with mAb-3305 before addition of rVSVs caused 228 a dose-dependent…

Lambe1, Maria Eugenia Dieterle2,‡, Kartik Chandran2, Rohit K. Jangra1,* 4 5 1 Department of Microbiology and Immunology, Center for Applied Immunology and 6 Pathological Processes, Center for Cardiovascular Diseases and Sciences, Louisiana 7 State University Health Sciences Center-Shreveport, Shreveport, Louisiana, USA. 8 2 Department of Microbiology and Immunology, Albert Einstein College of Medicine, 9 Bronx, New York, USA. 10 11 † Current address: Norgen Biotek, Thorold, Ontario, Canada. 12 ‡ Current address: Fundacion Instituto Leloir, Buenos Aires, Argentina. 13 14 * Corresponding author: Rohit K Jangra (rohit.jangra@lsuhs.edu) 15 16 17 Word counts: 18 19 Abstract: 243 20 Importance: 139 21 Text word count: 6367 22 Page 2 of 40 Abstract 23 Mammalian hantaviruses are RNA viruses that cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary 24 syndrome in the Americas and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Eurasia. The 25 cellular entry mechanisms of most hantaviruses remain poorly defined. To examine entry 26 by phylogenetically distinct hantaviruses, we generated replication-competent 27 recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses (rVSVs) bearing Gn/Gc proteins from Necoclí, 28 Sangassou, Thottapalayam, Kenkeme, Nova, Oxbow, and Tula viruses. All these Gn/Gc 29 proteins except Kenkeme supported infection of primary human endothelial cells, 30 indicating that endothelial cell entry is permissive for a broader range of hantaviruses than 31 previously appreciated. These three Gn/Gc proteins bound soluble PCDH1 with different 36 apparent avidities, and infection by the corresponding rVSVs was inhibited by soluble 37 PCDH1; Necoclí and Tula, but not Nova, were also blocked by a PCDH1-targeting 38 monoclonal antibody. Authentic Tula virus infection was similarly reduced in PCDH1 39 knockout endothelial cells. Finally, the broadly reactive anti-Gn/Gc human monoclonal 40 antibody ADI-42898 efficiently neutralized Necoclí, Nova, Sangassou, and Kenkeme 41 rVSVs but showed weak or undetectable activity against Oxbow, Tula, and Thottapalayam 42 rVSVs. An authentic Tula virus 55 experiment supports this conclusion beyond the surrogate system. Finally, a broadly 56 reactive anti-Gn/Gc antibody neutralizes several, but not all, of these viruses, highlighting 57 both the promise and the limits of broadly protective countermeasures and the utility of 58 these rVSVs for evaluating entry inhibitors. 59 60 Page 4 of 40 Introduction 61 Hantaviruses are enveloped, negative-sense RNA viruses that belong to the family 62 Hantaviridae in the order Elliovirales(1). papers.title: An ONT sequencing framework for hantavirus genome assembly, variant analysis, and defective viral genome characterization from whole-segment amplicons
papers.abstract: Orthohantaviruses are zoonotic, tri-segmented negative-sense RNA viruses of rodents and other small mammals that can cause severe human disease. Whole genome sequencing remains difficult because of low viral loads, high sequence diversity, and an inherent instability of the viral L segment. Current tiled amplicon and hybrid-capture approaches do not capture the heterogeneity of virus populations, including defective viral genomes (DVGs), which have never been described for hantaviruses. Here, we present an Oxford Nanopore Technologies sequencing framework based on universal reverse transcription primers targeting the conserved genome termini of orthohantaviruses and a single species-specific primer pair per segment, enabling amplification and sequencing of complete S, M, and L segments. We also developed an accompanying bioinformatic pipeline that performs reference-guided assembly of hantavirus genomes, consensus generation, variant calling, and DVG classification using the newly developed ORCHID classification pipeline. We applied this approach to diverse Puumala virus strains from infected cell cultures and bank voles, to representative Old World and New World orthohantaviruses, and to highly pathogenic New World viruses in vivo. In all cases we were able to accurately reconstruct full hantavirus genomes. Notably, we found that hantavirus populations contain highly abundant DVGs and conserved L segment deletions, whereas the S and M segments remained largely intact. Together, this work provides a low-cost, broadly applicable and easily customisable workflow for hantavirus genomics and reveals DVGs as a previously unrecognized feature of hantavirus populations.
