Current tiled amplicon and hybrid-capture 45 approaches do not capture the heterogeneity of virus populations, including defective 46 viral genomes (DVGs), which have never been described for hantaviruses. Here, we 47 present an Oxford Nanopore Technologies sequencing framework based on universal 48 reverse transcription primers targeting the conserved genome termini of 49 orthohantaviruses and a single species-specific primer pair per segment, enabling 50 amplification and sequencing of complete S, M, and L segments. We also developed an 51 accompanying bioinformatic pipeline that performs reference-guided assembly of 52 hantavirus genomes, consensus generation, variant calling, and DVG classification 53 using the newly developed ORCHID classification pipeline. We applied this approach to 54 diverse Puumala virus strains from infected cell cultures and bank voles, to 55 representative Old World and New World orthohantaviruses, and to highly pathogenic 56 New World viruses in vivo. In all cases we were able to accurately reconstruct full 57 hantavirus genomes. Notably, we found that hantavirus populations contain highly 58 abundant DVGs and conserved L segment deletions, whereas the S and M segments 59 remained largely intact. Together, this work provides a low-cost, broadly applicable and 60 easily customisable workflow for hantavirus genomics and reveals DVGs as a 61 previously unrecognized feature of hantavirus populations. 62 63 IMPORTANCE 64 Hantaviruses cause severe and often fatal human diseases, and their diversity and low 65 viral loads make them hard to sequence, which limits surveillance and outbreak 66 investigation. We describe a simple, universal but customisable, low-cost nanopore 67 sequencing workflow that recovers complete genome segments, including the full-length 68 L segment, from cell culture and animal tissues across the entire Orthohantavirus 69 genus. Using this approach, we report the first evidence of defective viral genomes in 70 hantaviruses. These truncated genomes arise mainly from the L segment, which 71 encodes the viral polymerase, and are formed at conserved genomic regions. Defective 72 viral genomes can modulate viral replication, innate immune activation, and persistence 73 in other viruses. Their presence in hantaviruses raises new questions about polymerase 74 function, tolerance in reservoir hosts, and immune-mediated disease in humans. Our 75 framework offers a practical tool for hantavirus genomics and a foundation for 76 investigating how defective genomes shape hantavirus infection. 77 3 INTRODUCTION 78 Orthohantaviruses (family Hantaviridae, class Bunyaviricetes) are zoonotic segmented 79 negative-sense RNA viruses that are naturally found in small mammal species, 80 including rodents, shrews, moles and bats (1). Human infections occur primarily through 81 inhalation of aerosolized excreta from infected animal hosts and can cause severe 82 disease, including haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and nephropathia 83 epidemica (NE) caused by Old World hantaviruses primarily in Eurasia and hantavirus 84 cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) caused by New World hantaviruses in the Americas 85 (2, 3). Case fatality rates for hantavirus diseases vary significantly depending on the 86 infecting virus species (4): it ranges from <1% for Puumala virus (PUUV), the causative 87 agent for NE, to up to 15% for HFRS-causing Old World hantaviruses such as Hantaan 88 virus (HTNV) in East Asia and Dobrava-Belgrade virus (DOBV) in eastern Europe, and 89 over 30% for HCPS-causing New World hantaviruses such as Andes virus (ANDV) and 90 Sin Nombre virus (SNV). 91 Hantaviruses have small tripartite negative-sense RNA genomes comprising the small 92 (S), medium (M) and large (L) genome segments, encoding only 4-5 viral proteins (5). 93 The S segment encodes the nucleoprotein (NP) and in some cases a non-structural 94 (NS) protein, the M segment encodes the glycoprotein precursor (GPC) which is co- 95 translationally cleaved into the Gn and Gc glycoproteins, and the L segment encodes 96 the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp). The genetic sequence divergence at the 97 amino acid level is significant across the hantavirus family (up to 75%) and even within 98 a species (up to 24%) (6). Low viral RNA copy numbers in clinical and rodent samples, 99 and natural RNA degradation outside of infected hosts makes obtaining complete 100 coverage of hantavirus genomes challenging (7, 8). Current state-of-the-art sequencing 101 approaches include metagenome sequencing, tiled amplicon sequencing and hybrid 102 capture-based sequencing, which all require extensive optimisation and large numbers 103 of probes (9–12). Existing long-read amplicon-based sequencing approaches often 104 include single amplicons for the smaller segments, but to date, there are no established 105 protocols to reliably capture the entire L segment in a single amplicon. In addition, while 106 these methods can provide full genome coverage sequencing and provide consensus 107 sequences of viruses, they do not accurately reflect the genetic makeup of any given 108 virus population. In reality, virus populations are highly heterogeneous and contain large 109 proportions of defective viral genomes (DVGs) consisting of genome truncations, 110 duplications and recombinations (13). However, DVGs have so far never been reported 111 for hantaviruses. 112 Here, we designed a whole segment amplicon-based long-read nanopore sequencing 113 method and an end-to-end bioinformatical analysis pipeline for hantavirus genome 114 assembly, alignment, consensus sequence generation, variant calling and defective 115 viral genome analysis (Fig.1A). This approach minimises required optimisation steps for 116 tiling and hybridization probes and enables a much more accurate depiction of 117 heterogenous virus populations without sacrificing sensitivity or genome coverage. 118 Using this method, we were able to sequence several diverse PUUV strains from both 119 infected cell cultures and from bank voles – their natural host species. In addition, we 120 validated our method using representative members of the whole Orthohantavirus 121 genus and samples obtained from cell cultures and animal tissues. Our sequencing 122 4 approach provides a cost-effective and rapid end-to-end pipeline to analyse hantavirus 123 genomes from environmental, animal and cellular samples. In addition, we provide the 124 first report of hantavirus DVGs and provide a framework for their analysis. 125 126 127 RESULTS 128 A nanopore sequencing and bioinformatics pipeline. Here, we designed a 129 whole segment amplicon-based long-read nanopore sequencing method. Hantavirus 130 RNA is reverse transcribed using universal hantavirus primers that hybridize with the 131 highly conserved 14 nucleotides at the genome termini. Subsequently, each genome 132 segment is amplified in a virus species-specific manner using a single longer primer pair 133 corresponding to the specific genome termini of a virus genome segment. PCR 134 products are then sequenced using Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) long-read 135 sequencing technology. This is followed by a bioinformatical analysis pipeline that 136 includes hantavirus reference-guided genome assembly, genome alignment, consensus 137 sequence generation, variant calling and DVG analysis (Fig.1A). The DVG analysis is 138 performed using the ‘ONT-based Recombination and Copy-back Haplotype 139 Identification for DVGs’ (ORCHID) pipeline which detects recombination events in virus 140 genomes and classifies these as artefacts, deletion, or copy-back events (Fig. 1B). 141 Deletion DVGs (delVGs) are produced when the RdRp dissociates from the genome 142 template during replication, continues reading the template without copying any of it, 143 and then reassociates and starts copying the template further downstream, thus 144 creating an internal deletion of the copied genome (Fig. 1C). Copy-back DVGs (cbVGs) 145 are produced when the RdRp dissociates from the template strand during replication 146 and reengages the nascent product strand as a new template (Fig. 1C). Together, this 147 workflow represents a highly customisable end-to-end sequencing and analysis 148 framework for hantaviruses. 149 150 Establishment of whole hantavirus segment amplification. While amplification 151 of the S and M segments in single amplicons has been achieved before, capturing the 152 entire L segment in one single amplicon has so far proven difficult (10). We utilized the 153 extremely high sequence conservation in the terminal 14 nucleotides of the 5’ and 3’ 154 ends of all three genome segments across the entire Orthohantavirus genus to design 155 universal hantavirus reverse transcription primers for both genomic negative-sense viral 156 RNA (vRNA) and the antigenomic positive-sense complementary RNA (cRNA) (Fig. 157 2A). Primers for amplification of individual segments also contained these highly 158 conserved termini but stretched further into the segments to achieve high specificity for 159 virus species and segments. 160 We established and optimised our virus species- and segment-specific viral genome 161 segment RT-PCR (vgsRT-PCR) method on RNA extracted from a cell-free purified 162 PUUV stock. First, we compared different RT primers and found that the Uni-c14 163 primer, random hexamers and oligo(dT) primers performed poorly and resulted in low or 164 no detectable amplification of PUUV segments (Fig. 2B). This was an expected result, 165 since hantaviruses generally are not thought to contain polyadenylation signals and 166 since the virus stock primarily should be composed of vRNA (14, 15). However, use of 167 5 the vRNA-specific Uni-v14 primer alone or in combination with the cRNA-specific Uni- 168 c14 primer yielded strong full-length amplification of all three PUUV segments. 169 Henceforth, the combination of vRNA- and cRNA-specific RT primers was used. Next, 170 different PCR elongation times and cycle numbers were compared. We observed that 171 for the longer L and M segments, increasing elongation time seemed to slightly increase 172 full-length segment amplification, while no major difference was observed for the S 173 segment (Fig. 2C). Based on these data we selected an elongation time of 3 min as the 174 best balance between sensitivity and overall reaction time. Increasing PCR cycle 175 numbers steadily increased PCR product accumulation in all three segments, with 176 robust product accumulation starting at 30 cycles (Fig 2D). As a compromise between 177 sensitivity, PCR bias and time optimisation, we chose 30 cycles as our default option, 178 with the possibility of increasing cycles to 40 for samples that require higher sensitivity. 179 As a proof-of-concept we also tested whether all segment-specific primers can be 180 combined in a single reaction and confirmed that all PUUV segments were efficiently 181 and equally amplified compared to the single primer pair reactions (Fig. 2E). Sensitivity 182 is important when designing PCR protocols for hantaviruses due to their inherently low 183 RNA copy numbers in infected patients. Using in vitro transcribed PUUV S segment 184 vRNA as a standard, we were able to accurately detect up to 101 RNA copies by RT- 185 qPCR (Fig. 2F) and up to 103 RNA copies by vgsRT-PCR (Fig. 2G). 186 Overall, we established a reproducible and sensitive vgsRT-PCR method for the optimal 187 amplification of whole PUUV segments with a single primer pair per segment. 188 189 Nanopore sequencing of diverse PUUV strains from cell culture. Having 190 established that we can robustly amplify full-length PUUV genomes, we next attempted 191 to sequence and characterise these amplicons from more complex samples by ONT 192 long-read sequencing. To that end, we infected human lung epithelial cells with several 193 different PUUV strains and extracted RNA from infected cells. First, we confirmed and 194 compared the presence of viral RNA by RT-qPCR and found robust – but varying – 195 levels of viral RNA in all samples (Fig.3A). Analysis of vgsRT-PCR products by gel 196 electrophoresis demonstrated clean amplification of the full M and S segments for all 197 PUUV strains (Fig. 3B). However, for the L segment we predominantly observed PCR 198 products of varying shorter lengths, suggesting production of internally truncated DVGs 199 that maintained the conserved segment termini. This was especially pronounced for the 200 PUUV strain BE/Cg/Villers-la-Tour/1/2009 (‘Villers-la-Tour’), BE/Cg/Seloignes/1/2009 201 (‘Seloignes’), BE/Cg/Beaumont/1/2012 (‘Beaumont’), and BE/Cg/Turnhout/1/1985 202 (‘Turnhout’), while RUS/Cg/Kazan/E6/1982 (‘Kazan-E6’) exhibited relatively clean full- 203 length products. Interestingly, while these putative DVGs exhibited strain-specific 204 profiles, the overall size distribution appears similar across all virus strains. 205 Nanopore sequencing of these amplicons demonstrated high levels of sequencing 206 depth across the entire genome (Table 1 and Fig. 3C). The genome coverage was even 207 across the entire genome for the M and S segments for all PUUV strains, confirming our 208 previous vgsRT-PCR data. Accordingly, we observed a striking reduction in genome 209 coverage in the central regions of the L segment for all strains except Kazan-E6, which 210 also did not generate any major truncated PCR products. We used the ORCHID 211 pipeline to classify sequenced viral reads and confirmed our vgsRT-PCR and genome 212 6 coverage data: while the M and S segments only contained small fractions of putative 213 and high-confidence DVGs, the vast majority of L segment reads were classified as 214 delVGs (Table 1 and Fig. 3D). Only Kazan-E6 exhibited a lower – yet still significant – 215 fraction of DVGs, consistent with our previous findings. As the M and S segments did 216 not exhibit any meaningful levels of DVGs, and cbVGs could not be detected at 217 significant levels in any segment, we characterized only L segment delVGs further. 218 Analysis of L segment delVG junction sizes revealed a now familiar pattern: while 219 Kazan-E6 only showed few unique junctions that were concentrated between 3000 and 220 4000 nt in size, all the remaining strains almost exclusively had very large 221 (approximately 4000 to 6000 nt in size) deletions (Fig. 3E). This helps explain why we 222 previously observed a relatively uniform pattern of truncated PCR products (Fig. 3B). 223 Investigation of the exact junction sites – i.e. at what nucleotide position of the genome 224 the RdRp disengages from the template (junction start) and then subsequently 225 reengages again (junction end) – helps shed further light onto the nature of these DVGs 226 and reveals highly specific regions in the PUUV L segment that are associated with 227 delVG formation (Fig. 3F). For the Turnhout, Beaumont, Seloignes and Villers-la-Tour 228 strains we observed highly similar patterns: the majority of deletions start within the first 229 100 nt of the 5’ end of the L segment and span almost the entire segment and end 230 within a more variable (approximately 1500 nt) window at the 3’ end of the segment 231 (Fig.3F). 232 Together, these data demonstrated that our whole segment amplicon sequencing 233 method is able to robustly sequence and resolve entire PUUV genomes. full_text_sections.full_text: 1 An ONT sequencing framework for hantavirus genome assembly, 1 variant analysis, and defective viral genome characterization from 2 whole-segment amplicons 3 4 Léna Vandenabeele1, Frances M. Twohig2, Anne Tuiskunen Bäck3,4,5,6, Magnus 5 Sjöblom7, Rebecca Lantto3, Gabriella Svala7, Janne Tynell8,9, Sandra Broddesson10,11, 6 Robert Dyrdak10,11, Wanda Christ1, Silke Riesle-Sbarbaro12, Joseph B. Prescott12, 7 Steven B. Bradfute2, Daniel P. Depledge13,14,15, Benjamin E. Nilsson-Payant1 8 9 1 Division of Virology and Immunology, Department of Microbiology, Tumor and Cell 10 Biology, Karolinska Institutet, Stockholm, Sweden 11 2 Department of Internal Medicine, Center for Global Health, University of New Mexico 12 Health Sciences Center, Albuquerque, New Mexico, United States of America 13 3 Department of Clinical Microbiology, Umeå University, Umeå, Sweden 14 4 Department of Public Health and Clinical Medicine, Umeå University, Umeå, Sweden 15 5 Umeå Centre for Microbial Research (UCMR), Umeå University, Umeå, Sweden 16 6 Laboratory for Molecular Infection Medicine Sweden (MIMS), Umeå University, Umeå, 17 Sweden 18 7 Clinical Microbiology Unit, Department of Laboratory Medicine, Sunderby Hospital, 19 Luleå, Sweden 20 8 Department of Virology, University of Helsinki, Helsinki, Finland 21 9 Institute of Biomedicine, University of Turku, Turku, Finland 22 10 Division of Clinical Genomics & Virology, Department of Microbiology, Tumor and Cell 23 Biology, Karolinska Institutet, Stockholm, Sweden 24 11 Department of Clinical Microbiology, Karolinska University Hospital, Stockholm, 25 Sweden 26 12 Center for Biological Threats and Special Pathogens, Robert Koch Institute, Berlin, 27 Germany 28 13 Institute of Virology, Hannover Medical School, Hannover, Germany 29 14 Cluster of Excellence RESIST (EXC 2155), Hannover Medical School, Hannover 30 Germany 31 15 German Center for Infection Research (DZIF), partner site Hannover-Braunschweig, 32 Hannover, Germany 33 34 35 Corresponding author: benjamin.nilssonpayant@ki.se 36 37 38 39 40 2 ABSTRACT 41 Orthohantaviruses are zoonotic, tri-segmented negative-sense RNA viruses of rodents 42 and other small mammals that can cause severe human disease. Whole genome 43 sequencing remains difficult because of low viral loads, high sequence diversity, and an 44 inherent instability of the viral L segment. Current tiled amplicon and hybrid-capture 45 approaches do not capture the heterogeneity of virus populations, including defective 46 viral genomes (DVGs), which have never been described for hantaviruses. Here, we 47 present an Oxford Nanopore Technologies sequencing framework based on universal 48 reverse transcription primers targeting the conserved genome termini of 49 orthohantaviruses and a single species-specific primer pair per segment, enabling 50 amplification and sequencing of complete S, M, and L segments. We also developed an 51 accompanying bioinformatic pipeline that performs reference-guided assembly of 52 hantavirus genomes, consensus generation, variant calling, and DVG classification 53 using the newly developed ORCHID classification pipeline. We applied this approach to 54 diverse Puumala virus strains from infected cell cultures and bank voles, to 55 representative Old World and New World orthohantaviruses, and to highly pathogenic 56 New World viruses in vivo. In all cases we were able to accurately reconstruct full 57 hantavirus genomes. Notably, we found that hantavirus populations contain highly 58 abundant DVGs and conserved L segment deletions, whereas the S and M segments 59 remained largely intact. Together, this work provides a low-cost, broadly applicable and 60 easily customisable workflow for hantavirus genomics and reveals DVGs as a 61 previously unrecognized feature of hantavirus populations. 62 63 IMPORTANCE 64 Hantaviruses cause severe and often fatal human diseases, and their diversity and low 65 viral loads make them hard to sequence, which limits surveillance and outbreak 66 investigation. We describe a simple, universal but customisable, low-cost nanopore 67 sequencing workflow that recovers complete genome segments, including the full-length 68 L segment, from cell culture and animal tissues across the entire Orthohantavirus 69 genus. Using this approach, we report the first evidence of defective viral genomes in 70 hantaviruses. These truncated genomes arise mainly from the L segment, which 71 encodes the viral polymerase, and are formed at conserved genomic regions. Defective 72 viral genomes can modulate viral replication, innate immune activation, and persistence 73 in other viruses. Their presence in hantaviruses raises new questions about polymerase 74 function, tolerance in reservoir hosts, and immune-mediated disease in humans. Our 75 framework offers a practical tool for hantavirus genomics and a foundation for 76 investigating how defective genomes shape hantavirus infection. 77 3 INTRODUCTION 78 Orthohantaviruses (family Hantaviridae, class Bunyaviricetes) are zoonotic segmented 79 negative-sense RNA viruses that are naturally found in small mammal species, 80 including rodents, shrews, moles and bats (1). Human infections occur primarily through 81 inhalation of aerosolized excreta from infected animal hosts and can cause severe 82 disease, including haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and nephropathia 83 epidemica (NE) caused by Old World hantaviruses primarily in Eurasia and hantavirus 84 cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) caused by New World hantaviruses in the Americas 85 (2, 3). Case fatality rates for hantavirus diseases vary significantly depending on the 86 infecting virus species (4): it ranges from <1% for Puumala virus (PUUV), the causative 87 agent for NE, to up to 15% for HFRS-causing Old World hantaviruses such as Hantaan 88 virus (HTNV) in East Asia and Dobrava-Belgrade virus (DOBV) in eastern Europe, and 89 over 30% for HCPS-causing New World hantaviruses such as Andes virus (ANDV) and 90 Sin Nombre virus (SNV). 91 Hantaviruses have small tripartite negative-sense RNA genomes comprising the small 92 (S), medium (M) and large (L) genome segments, encoding only 4-5 viral proteins (5). 93 The S segment encodes the nucleoprotein (NP) and in some cases a non-structural 94 (NS) protein, the M segment encodes the glycoprotein precursor (GPC) which is co- 95 translationally cleaved into the Gn and Gc glycoproteins, and the L segment encodes 96 the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp). The genetic sequence divergence at the 97 amino acid level is significant across the hantavirus family (up to 75%) and even within 98 a species (up to 24%) (6). Low viral RNA copy numbers in clinical and rodent samples, 99 and natural RNA degradation outside of infected hosts makes obtaining complete 100 coverage of hantavirus genomes challenging (7, 8). Current state-of-the-art sequencing 101 approaches include metagenome sequencing, tiled amplicon sequencing and hybrid 102 capture-based sequencing, which all require extensive optimisation and large numbers 103 of probes (9–12). Existing long-read amplicon-based sequencing approaches often 104 include single amplicons for the smaller segments, but to date, there are no established 105 protocols to reliably capture the entire L segment in a single amplicon. In addition, while 106 these methods can provide full genome coverage sequencing and provide consensus 107 sequences of viruses, they do not accurately reflect the genetic makeup of any given 108 virus population. In reality, virus populations are highly heterogeneous and contain large 109 proportions of defective viral genomes (DVGs) consisting of genome truncations, 110 duplications and recombinations (13). However, DVGs have so far never been reported 111 for hantaviruses. 112 Here, we designed a whole segment amplicon-based long-read nanopore sequencing 113 method and an end-to-end bioinformatical analysis pipeline for hantavirus genome 114 assembly, alignment, consensu…

analysis_zh.background: 正汉坦病毒es 是人畜共患的、三段负链RNA病毒,寄宿于啮齿动物及其他小型哺乳动物,可导致严重的人类疾病。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者开发了一种Oxford Nanopore Technologies工作流程,使用针对保守基因组末端的通用逆转录引物以及每段的单一物种特异性引物对,结合参考引导的生物信息学管线进行组装、共识生成、变异检测和缺陷病毒基因组(DVG)分类;该方法应用于来自感染细胞培养和田鼠的多样化 普马拉病毒 株系,以及代表性的旧世界和新世界 正汉坦病毒es,包括体内高度致病的新世界病毒。

analysis_zh.contribution: 该低成本、广泛适用的工作流程实现了对 汉坦病毒 的全面基因组学研究,并揭示DVG是 汉坦病毒 群体先前未被识别的特征。

papers.title: Vascular Programs in Emerging and Re-Emerging RNA Virus Infections: Comparative Lessons from SARS-CoV-2, Flaviviruses, and Hantaviruses
papers.abstract: Emerging and re-emerging RNA viruses frequently present with clinical phenotypes that extend beyond classical organ tropism and include vascular leakage, platelet dysregulation, coagulation imbalance, microvascular injury, and thromboinflammation. SARS-CoV-2, flaviviruses, and hantaviruses provide three complementary models of virus-induced vascular disease. This narrative review compares these viruses through a shared endothelial–coagulative framework and proposes four partially overlapping vascular programs: endothelial activation, endothelial barrier failure, coagulation activation, and platelet quantitative or qualitative dysfunction. These programs are intended as a conceptual synthesis of convergent clinical, pathological, and experimental evidence rather than as a quantitative classification system. The framework is used not only to organize known mechanisms, but also to generate testable predictions for cross-virus biomarker panels, organ-specific endothelial models, and phenotype-guided clinical studies. Severe COVID-19 illustrates inflammation-driven endothelial activation, platelet–leukocyte interactions, complement amplification, NETosis, and immunothrombosis. Within the flavivirus group, DENV is used as the principal model for systemic vascular leakage, thrombocytopenia, and hemorrhagic risk; selected non-dengue flaviviruses illustrate how shared endothelial, platelet, and coagulation modules are redirected toward placental dysfunction (ZIKV), neuroinvasion (WNV and JEV), or hepatic failure and coagulopathy (YFV). Hantavirus infections provide a distinctive model of capillary leak syndrome in which non-lytic endothelial infection, immune-mediated injury, and permeability signaling converge on renal and pulmonary microvascular beds. A comparative view suggests that thrombotic, hemorrhagic, and leaky phenotypes are not mutually exclusive categories, but different outcomes of overlapping vascular programs shaped by viral tropism, vascular-bed specialization, immune activation, and host susceptibility.

analysis.background: Emerging and re‑emerging RNA viruses often cause vascular leakage, platelet dysregulation, coagulation imbalance, microvascular injury, and thromboinflammation, prompting a focused review (A1).
analysis.main_directions: The authors compare SARS‑CoV‑2, flaviviruses, and hantaviruses as complementary models and organize disease into four overlapping vascular programs—endothelial activation, barrier failure, coagulation activation, and platelet dysfunction (A2, A3).
analysis.current_state: Severe COVID‑19 shows inflammation‑driven endothelial activation and immunothrombosis; dengue illustrates systemic leakage and thrombocytopenia; other flaviviruses redirect shared vascular modules toward placental, neuro, or hepatic pathology; hantaviruses produce capillary‑leak syndromes via non‑lytic infection and immune injury (A6‑A10).
analysis.gaps: The vascular programs are presented as a conceptual synthesis without quantitative validation, limiting their precision for classification or prediction (A4).
analysis.future_research: The framework is proposed to guide the development of cross‑virus biomarker panels, organ‑specific endothelial models, and phenotype‑guided clinical studies (A5).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Emerging RNA viruses cause vascular complications beyond organ tropism (A1). Main directions: SARS‑CoV‑2, flaviviruses, and hantaviruses are compared within four overlapping vascular programs (A2, A3). Current state: COVID‑19, dengue, other flaviviruses, and hantaviruses each exemplify distinct but intersecting endothelial, platelet, and coagulation disturbances (A6‑A10). Gaps: The proposed programs lack quantitative validation (A4). Future research: Use the framework to develop cross‑virus biomarker panels, organ‑specific endothelial models, and phenotype‑guided clinical studies (A5).

papers.title_zh: 新发与再发RNA病毒感染中的血管程序:来自SARS‐CoV‐2、黄病毒及汉坦病毒的比较经验

analysis_zh.background: 新发和再发RNA病毒常导致血管渗漏、血小板功能失调、凝血失衡、微血管损伤和血栓炎症,因而进行聚焦综述 (A1)。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 作者将SARS‐CoV‐2、黄病毒以及汉坦病毒es 作为互补模型进行比较,并将疾病划分为四个相互重叠的血管程序——内皮激活、屏障失效、凝血激活和血小板功能障碍 (A2, A3)。
analysis_zh.current_state: 重症COVID‐19表现为炎症驱动的内皮激活和免疫血栓形成;登革热表现为全身渗漏和血小板减少;其他黄病毒将共享的血管模块重定向至胎盘、神经或肝脏病理;汉坦病毒es 通过非溶细胞感染和免疫损伤导致毛细血管渗漏综合征 (A6‐A10)。
analysis_zh.gaps: 血管程序以概念性综合呈现,缺乏定量验证,限制了其在分类或预测中的精确性 (A4)。
analysis_zh.future_research: 该框架旨在指导跨病毒生物标志物面板、器官特异性内皮模型以及表型导向的临床研究的开发 (A5)。

papers.summary_zh: 背景:新发和再发RNA病毒常导致血管渗漏、血小板功能失调、凝血失衡、微血管损伤和血栓炎症,因而进行聚... 主要方向:作者将SARS‐CoV‐2、黄病毒以及汉坦病毒es 作为互补模型进行比较,并将疾病划分为四个相... 研究现状:重症COVID‐19表现为炎症驱动的内皮激活和免疫血栓形成;登革热表现为全身渗漏和血小板减少;... 不足:血管程序以概念性综合呈现,缺乏定量验证,限制了其在分类或预测中的精确性 (A4)。 后续研究:该框架旨在指导跨病毒生物标志物面板、器官特异性内皮模型以及表型导向的临床研究的开发 (A5)。

papers.title: IDENTIFICATION OF A STRUCTURALLY AND EVOLUTIONARILY CONSERVED 3'→5' PROOFREADING EXONUCLEASE DOMAIN IN THE LARGE L PROTEIN OF HANTAVIRUSES- EMERGING HUMAN PATHOGENS
papers.abstract: The proofreading 3′→5′ exonuclease not only represents a crucial class of enzymes responsible for maintaining genome integrity across diverse groups of organisms, but also plays a critical role in ensuring replication fidelity. In the non-segmented, positive-strand bat-borne RNA viruses like Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronaviruses (SARS-CoVs and MERS-CoV), it is found along with the methyltransferase (MTase) gene of the non-structural protein 14 (NSP14). In contrast, in the non-segmented, but negative-strand bat-borne RNA viruses such as Marburg, Ebola and Nipah viruses, it has been identified together with a novel type of capping enzyme, viz. guanosine diphosphate polyribonucleotidyltransferase (PRNTase). Hantaviruses, one of the fatal and emerging human pathogens in recent times, belong to segmented, negative-strand RNA viruses and are primarily rodent-borne. Currently, no universally approved vaccine or antiviral therapy exists for all hantavirus infections. The presence of a proofreading (PR) exonuclease domain has not been reported in hantaviruses until now. Interestingly, a putative PR exonuclease domain has been identified for the first time in these viruses within the large L protein, preceding the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp). The newly identified domain belongs to the DEDD superfamily, but exhibits a distinct structural deviation, notably the replacement of the first catalytic triad -DxE- in the Old World hantaviruses with an -NxE- motif in most of the New World hantaviruses, and the use of an invariant tyrosine instead of histidine at the proton acceptor site. This feature closely resembles the DEDD superfamily of PR exonucleases reported in bacterial DNA polymerases I and II and in the DNA-dependent DNA polymerases of DNA viruses. To the best of my knowledge, this study provides the first evidence for the presence of a typical DEDD superfamily of PR exonuclease domain in hantaviruses, and thus, expanding our understanding of the structure and catalytic mechanism of 3′→5′ PR exonucleases in segmented, negative-strand RNA viruses and further presenting a novel structural target for the development of universally effective antiviral therapies against fatal hantavirus infections.
papers.journal: World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews

World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews, 2026, 32(01), 969–979 970 1 INTRODUCTION Viruses are ubiquitous in nature, infecting and proliferating in organisms across all kingdoms of life. They have evolved and adapted their lifecycles to the organisms they infect and, following successful infection, viruses rely predominantly on their host’s cellular machinery for their survival and proliferation. Based on the nature of their genome, viruses are broadly classified into RNA and DNA viruses. Both types cause diseases in plants, animals and humans, ranging from endemic to pandemic proportions, resulting in major global healthcare crises and unprecedented economic losses, necessitating a deeper understanding of their pathogenic and replication mechanisms to develop effective therapeutic interventions [1]. However, the majority of the serious human diseases are caused by RNA viruses belonging to both negative- and positive-strand viruses [2]. For example, Measles, Mumps, Human influenza viruses (A, B and C), Hendra, Cedar, Ebola, Marburg, Nipah, Rabies, etc. are caused by the non-segmented, negative-strand RNA viruses whereas SARS-CoVs, MERS-CoV, Polio, Hepatitis C, Dengue, Zika, Yellow fever, Rubella, Encephalomyocarditis, HIVs, etc. belong to non-segmented, but positive-strand RNA viruses. Again, some of the RNA viruses possess segmented, single-stranded genomes like human influenza viruses (8 segments) and hantaviruses (3 segments), whereas some possess segmented, double-stranded RNA genomes like rotavirus and bluetongue virus. Hantaviruses are emerging human pathogens that cause severe, often fatal, hemorrhagic fevers and pulmonary syndromes. They have been responsible for several human disease outbreaks in recent years. Furthermore, human-to- human transmission in recent years has established hantaviruses as one of the most dangerous viruses [3, 4]. In fact, hantaviruses are more serious and lethal than the SARS-CoV-2, as some of them have a greater mortality rate (~50%) than the latter (~1% global average). Mostly hantaviruses are not transmitted between humans. However, the Andes orthohantavirus in South America has demonstrated limited person-to-person transmission, particularly among those in close contact. For example, recently, an outbreak of the Andes orthohantavirus on a cruise ship infected 11 people and killed three earlier this year (2026). Hantavirus was first discovered following the Korean War. During the war, haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) was a common ailment in soldiers stationed near the Hantan River. This illness is now considered as one of the most serious haemorrhagic diseases in the world, like Ebola haemorrhagic fever, due to its high mortality rate and epidemic potential. The first hantavirus was isolated in 1978 in South Korea and was named Hantaan virus. Based on the geographic distribution, hantaviruses are broadly classified into Old World hantaviruses, which typically cause HFRS and are prevalent in Africa, Asia, and Europe, (e.g., Hantaan virus, Seoul virus, Puumala virus, Dobrava-Belgrade virus, Amur virus, etc.) and New World hantaviruses (e.g., Andes virus, Sin Nombre virus, Laguna Negra virus, Black Creek Canal virus, Choclo virus, etc.) which are associated with hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) in the Americas [5, 6]. The hantaviruses are primarily rodent-borne and are the main source of human infections, although new hantaviruses have recently been reported or isolated from bats, moles and shrews [7, 8]. Spillover of these viruses to humans can result in one of the two serious illnesses. The case fatality rate of HFRS ranges from 1% to 15%, while for HPS, it is 30–60% [9]. Thus, both diseases can be fatal, but with differing mortality rates. Currently, there is neither an approved vaccine nor a specific and effective antiviral treatment available for human use. Importantly, hantaviruses can survive for 10 days at room temperature, 15 days in temperate environments and more than 18 days at 4 °C (39 °F), which facilitates their stable transmission [9, 10]. Therefore, understanding the structure of the hantavirus genome and the functions of the key viral proteins is critical for developing effective antiviral therapeutic agents to control the spread of the virus. 1.1 Classification of hantaviruses Hantaviruses belong to the genus Orthohantavirus and the order Bunyavirales within the family of Hantaviridae. They are enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses that cause two potentially lethal zoonotic syndromes, viz. HFRS and HPS as discussed elsewhere. It is estimated that, globally, around 1.5 million people get infected with hantaviruses each year with typical case fatality rates of up to 15 % for HFRS and around 40 % or higher for HPS [11]. Hantaviruses are further classified into Old World (HFRS-causing) and New World (HPS-causing) viruses [3]. The Old World hantaviruses are primarily found in Europe and Asia and typically cause HFRS with a mortality rate of up to 15%. Examples include, Hantaan virus, Seoul virus, Puumala virus, Dobrava-Belgrade virus, Amur virus, etc. The New World hantaviruses are more dangerous and prevalent in North and South America and are associated with HPS with mortality rates reaching up to 40%. Examples include, Sin Nombre virus, Andes virus, Laguna Negra virus, Black Creek Canal virus. Choclo virus, etc. [12]. Among the hantaviruses, only the New World Andes virus has been demonstrated to have the potential for human-to-human transmission [4]. 1.2 3’→5’ PR exonucleases and their classifications PR exonucleases (EC 3.1.11.x) are ubiquitous enzymes that play a crucial role in repairing error(s) during replication of genomes and thus, maintain the integrity of genomes in organisms. They remove misincorporated wrong nucleotides in the 3′→ 5′ direction during DNA/RNA synthesis. Based on their conserved active site amino acids, these enzymes are broadly classified into two superfamilies, viz. the DEDD and the Polymerase and Histidinol Phosphatase (PHP) superfamilies [13, 14]. The DEDD superfamily is the most common type of PR enzyme and is reported from both DNA World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews, 2026, 32(01), 969–979 971 and RNA polymerases from a large number of organisms from viruses to humans. The name derives from the four highly conserved acidic amino acid residues, viz. DEDD, in its active site for metal-binding and catalysis. The PHP superfamily, characterized by the active site amino acid structure, HxH-E-H-D, uses His residues for metal-binding and catalysis. Bacterial/Archaeal DNA polymerases X, bacterial DNA polymerases III (bacterial replicases) with a co-editing, built-in exonuclease [14, 15] and YcdX phosphoesterases [16] belong to PHP superfamily. Both superfamilies are essentially Zn- dependent enzymes and initiate the catalysis from a metal-bound water molecule [17]. It is interesting to note that certain viruses like the human influenza viruses use both types of PR exonucleases [18]. Furthermore, the DEDD superfamily is further classified into two subfamilies, viz. DEDD(Y) and DEDD(H), depending on whether they employ an invariant Y or a H as the proton acceptor during catalysis [Table 1]. Most of the RNA and DNA viruses possess a typical DEDD superfamily of 3′→5′ PR exoribonuclease in their genome and are well-characterized. For example, in SARS-CoVs and MERS-CoV, it is characterized in the ExoN of the non-structural protein 14 along with the methyltransferase domain [17]. But in the other bat-borne viruses such as Marburg, Ebola and Nipah, a DEDD superfamily of PR exonuclease domain was identified in the PRNTase (the capping enzyme) domain [19]. The DEDD superfamily of PR exonuclease has also been reported in DNA viruses like smallpox, monkeypox viruses, etc. [Table 1] suggesting the same PR mechanism is used by both types of viruses. In contrast to their ubiquitous presence in RNA and DNA viruses, in hantaviruses it was reported that there was no demonstrated, dedicated proofreading exonuclease [20, 21]. However, in the present communication, a putative DEDD superfamily of PR exonuclease domain, preceding the RdRp domain, has been identified featuring an invariant Y as the proton acceptor. 1.3 Importance of 3ʹ→5ʹ PR exonuclease as a potential drug target for controlling RNA viruses Maintenance of genome stability is essential for all living organisms and it mainly relies on the error-free replication of genomes by the respective DNA and RNA replicases. The genome stability is equally important for viruses also. This is because too many uncorrected mutations during replications could lead to an "error catastrophe," where the viruses could literally mutate itself to death. To overcome this problem, the RNA and DNA polymerases/replicases exhibit strong discrimination between nucleoside triphosphates (NTPs) and deoxynucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs) and rarely insert a wrong nucleotide during replication of genomes and hence, their error rates are very, very low and is usually in the order of ~10-4 to 10-6 and ~10-6-10-9, respectively [22]. To overcome even this minimal error rates during replications, these crucial polymerases of life are invariably associated with PR mechanisms that correct any insertion error(s) during replication. When an incorrect nucleotide gets incorporated during replication, the polymerases stall/pause, which in-turn activates the associated PR function, which promptly excises the misincorporated nucleotide. The DEDD superfamily of PR exonucleases operates in the 3’→5’ direction and excise any incorrectly incorporated nucleotide from the 3’-growing end, and thus, helping the polymerases to perform error-free replication of genomes. Following the excision of the wrong nucleotide, the correct nucleotide is inserted and the polymerases resume the replication. This critical PR step in living organisms and viruses ensures that the original DNA/RNA template is copied accurately and passed on to the next generation. For example, with the PR 3'→ 5' exonuclease activity, the error rate dramatically improves to an accuracy of about 10−7 to 10−8 (one mistake per 10 million to 100 million bases). And further, with cellular mismatch repair, the final error rate drops as low as 10−9 to 10−11 per base pair (i.e., about one mistake per 1 billion bases) [23]. Thus, the PR functions play a crucial role in maintaining the integrity of genomes in all organisms including the viruses. It is interesting to note that a SARS-CoV-2 PR exonuclease knockout mutant was unable to replicate, suggesting possibilities for development of effective antivirals directing the PR exonucleases to contain the spread of RNA viruses [17]. 1.4 Genome and L protein organizations in hantaviruses Arenaviridae, Bunyaviridae, and Orthomyxoviridae are the principal families of segmented, negative-strand RNA viruses, and each of them include serious human pathogens. Arenaviridae have two genome segments, whereas Bunyaviridae and Orthomyxoviridae have three and six to eight genome segments, respectively. Arenaviruses and bunyaviruses replicate in the cytoplasm using a single subunit RdRp of the L protein, whereas the orthomyxoviruses replicate in the nucleus- an unusual trait of an RNA virus- using a heterotrimeric polymerase complex composed of PA, PB1 and PB2 subunits [18]. Hantaviruses are segmented, negative-strand, enveloped viruses which belong to the order Bunyavirales, Family, Hantaviridae, and Genus, Orthohantavirus. Unlike other human pathogenic viruses, they are primarily carried by rodents. The virions are generally spherical to pleomorphic, measuring approximately 80-160 nm in diameter, although the size may vary among species. Thus, the segmented, tripartite RNA genome of hantaviruses consists of a small (S), a medium (M), and a large (L) segment and encodes only four structural proteins. The S segment encodes the nucleocapsid (N) protein, which encapsidates viral RNA genome segments to form ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes and plays key roles in viral replication and immune modulation. The M segment encodes a glycoprotein precursor that is post-translationally cleaved into two envelope glycoproteins, Gn and Gc, which are essential for viral attachment and entry into host cells. The multidomain L segment encodes a viral RdRp, responsible for both transcription and replication and a cap- snatching endonuclease, responsible for snatching mRNA caps from the host mRNAs for priming the viral mRNAs. The World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews, 2026, 32(01), 969–979 972 genomic RNA segments are encapsidated by the nucleocapsid protein P, to form helical RNP complexes, which are enclosed within a host-derived lipid envelope studded with Gn and Gc glycoprotein spikes. [24]. The viral envelope is derived from host cell membranes and contains the above embedded glycoprotein spikes that facilitate interaction with host cell receptors. The tripartite genome segments form into circles via non-covalent interactions of the ends of the genome with an attached L protein to initiate transcription upon entry into host cells. The 3'- and 5'- terminal nucleotides are highly conserved and complementary in all three genome segments that form a conserved panhandle structure acting as the viral promoter in each of the genome segment. In addition to the coding region, each segment possesses short untranslated regions (UTRs) at the 5′ and 3′ termini. The 3' and 5' UTRs are highly conserved and regulate replication and transcription of the genomes [25]. papers.title: Development of a rapid RPA-CRISPR/Cas12b assay for dual detection of Hantaan virus and Seoul virus.
papers.abstract: Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) are the primary causative agents of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), presenting a persistent challenge to global public health. Prompt and precise diagnostic tools are essential for clinical investigation and the containment of HFRS outbreaks. Leveraging the programmable precision of CRISPR/Cas12b system, which has significantly advanced the field of molecular diagnostics, we developed a rapid, high-sensitivity assay for the dual detection of HTNV and SEOV. Each virus was detected in a separate, target-specific single-tube reaction. The assay combines recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) with CRISPR/Cas12b-mediated fluorescence detection and uses virus-specific sgRNAs and RPA primers targeting conserved genomic regions. Using recombinant plasmid standards, both targets were detected at 1 × 10 1 copies/test in three technical replicates; this is a preliminary analytical detection threshold and does not incorporate extraction losses or matrix-associated inhibition. No cross-reactivity was observed within the evaluated four-organism non-target panel. In a preliminary feasibility assessment, all nine RT-qPCR-positive rodent samples (seven HTNV and two SEOV) were positive by the RPA-CRISPR/Cas12b assay, indicating complete positive agreement in this all-positive sample set. Because no negative samples were included, negative agreement, diagnostic specificity, false-positive rate, and overall clinical diagnostic accuracy could not be assessed. These results support further development of the assay as a potential screening tool; larger studies using well-characterized positive and negative clinical or field specimens are required.

papers.title_zh: 开发一种快速RPA-CRISPR/Cas12b检测方法,用于双重检测汉滩病毒和首尔病毒。

analysis_zh.background: 汉滩病毒(HTNV)和首尔病毒(SEOV)是肾综合征出血热的主要致病因素,这是一项持续的全球公共卫生挑战。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者设计了一种单管RPA‐CRISPR/Cas12b检测,使用针对保守区域的病毒特异性sgRNA和引物;通过重组质粒标准评估了分析灵敏度,并在九个RT‐qPCR阳性的啮齿动物样本上测试了可行性;未报告研究地点和宿主细节。
analysis_zh.results: 该检测在三次重复中最低可检测到每次测试10拷贝,未出现对四种非目标生物的交叉反应,并在九个啮齿动物样本中与RT‐qPCR实现了100 %阳性一致性;阴性一致性无法评估。
analysis_zh.contribution: 这些发现展示了一种快速、高灵敏度的双重检测平台,可作为HFRS监测和临床研究的筛查工具。
analysis_zh.limitations: 检测限未考虑提取损失或基质抑制,未纳入阴性样本导致特异性和整体诊断准确性仍未知,且仅有摘要数据可用。

papers.title: Computational Evaluation of a Novel Nitrothiophene-Derived Schiff Base Ligand Against Breast Cancer-Associated Proteins and Andes Hantavirus Nucleoprotein: Molecular Docking and ADMET Analysis
papers.abstract: The identification of small molecules capable of interacting with multiple therapeutically relevant protein targets is an important strategy in early-stage drug discovery. In the present study, the Schiff base ligand ((N1E,N8E)-N1,N8-bis((5-nitrothiophen-2-yl)methylene)naphthalene-1,8-diamine; N1) was computationally evaluated against a panel of representative disease-associated proteins to investigate its target-binding profile. The primary focus was the assessment of N1 against breast cancer-associated receptor kinases, including EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K, which play central roles in oncogenic signaling pathways. In addition, the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein was included as an exploratory antiviral target to examine the broader target recognition capability of the ligand rather than to propose a common therapeutic mechanism. Molecular docking studies were performed using AutoDock Vina with experimentally determined protein structures obtained from the Protein Data Bank. N1 demonstrated favorable binding affinities toward all investigated breast cancer targets, with docking scores of −8.708 kcal/mol for EGFR, −8.836 kcal/mol for HER2, −8.906 kcal/mol for VEGFR2, and −9.066 kcal/mol for PI3K. The ligand also exhibited a docking score of −8.8 kcal/mol against the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein. Interaction analysis revealed multiple stabilizing hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic contacts, electrostatic interactions, and π-mediated interactions within the respective binding pockets.Drug-likeness assessment indicated compliance with Lipinski's and Ghose's rules, while ADMET prediction suggested favorable absorption and membrane permeability. Nevertheless, the predicted risks of hepatotoxicity, cardiotoxicity, and mutagenicity indicate that further structural optimization and experimental validation are required. Overall, this study demonstrates the potential of N1 as a promising scaffold for breast cancer-associated kinase inhibition while providing preliminary evidence of its broader protein-binding capability across biologically distinct targets.

Keywords: Breast cancer, Hantavirus, Molecular docking, Drug-likeness, ADMET, Schiff base Cite This Article: Temitayo O. Aiyelabola, Sayantan Pradhan, and Takashiro Akitsu, “Computational Evaluation of a Novel Nitrothiophene-Derived Schiff Base Ligand Against Breast Cancer-Associated Proteins and Andes Hantavirus Nucleoprotein: Molecular Docking and ADMET Analysis.” Journal of Polymer and Biopolymer Physics Chemistry, vol. 14, no. 1 (2026): 1-14. doi: 10.12691/jpbpc-14-1-1. 1. Introduction Cancer and viral infections remain among the most serious global health challenges due to their high mortality rates, rapid disease progression, and limited availability of effective therapeutic agents [1,2]. Among different malignancies, breast cancer is one of the most frequently diagnosed cancers and represents a leading cause of cancer-related death among women worldwide [3]. The development and progression of breast cancer are closely associated with abnormal activation of receptor tyrosine kinases and intracellular signaling proteins, particularly Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR), Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2 (HER2), Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor Receptor 2 (VEGFR2), and phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) [4,5,6]. These signaling proteins regulate essential cellular processes such as proliferation, angiogenesis, migration, metastasis, survival, and apoptosis. Overexpression or mutation of these targets has been strongly linked with aggressive tumor 2 Journal of Polymer and Biopolymer Physics Chemistry progression and poor clinical prognosis [7]. EGFR and HER2 activation initiates downstream signaling cascades, including the RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK and PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathways, which contribute to uncontrolled cancer cell proliferation, enhanced survival, and metastatic progression (Figure 1) [8,9]. VEGFR2 plays a crucial role in tumor angiogenesis by stimulating endothelial cell migration and vascular formation necessary for tumor growth and metastasis [10]. PI3K, a central component of the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway, regulates cellular growth, proliferation, metabolism, and survival and is frequently dysregulated in breast cancer [11]. Collectively, EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K represent interconnected signaling proteins that regulate complementary aspects of breast cancer progression, including cell proliferation, survival, angiogenesis, and metastasis. Since these proteins belong to functionally linked oncogenic signaling networks, their simultaneous computational evaluation provides an opportunity to investigate whether a single chemical scaffold can potentially interact with multiple biologically relevant targets involved in breast cancer. It should be noted that the present study aims to explore the binding characteristics of N1 toward these proteins through molecular docking and does not imply experimentally validated inhibition of these signaling pathways. Therefore, EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K were selected as representative breast cancer-associated targets for an exploratory computational target-profiling study (Figure 1) [8,9,10,11]. In addition to cancer, viral infections caused by emerging and re-emerging viruses continue to pose major public health concerns worldwide. Andes hantavirus, a member of the Hantaviridae family, is responsible for hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), a severe respiratory disease associated with high fatality rates [12]. The viral nucleoprotein (N protein) plays an essential role in viral RNA encapsidation, ribonucleoprotein complex formation, genome replication, and viral assembly, making it a biologically relevant target for antiviral drug discovery (Figure 2) [13]. Unlike viral enzymes, the nucleoprotein does not possess catalytic activity; instead, its RNA-binding region is responsible for recognizing and stabilizing viral genomic RNA during ribonucleoprotein assembly. Accordingly, the molecular docking analysis in the present study focused on this functionally important RNA-binding region to evaluate the potential molecular recognition of N1. Binding at this site may theoretically interfere with RNA recognition or ribonucleoprotein assembly; however, such effects remain computational hypotheses that require experimental validation [13,14]. The inclusion of the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein was intended as an exploratory assessment of the binding versatility of the N1 scaffold against a structurally unrelated viral target rather than to propose a unified therapeutic strategy linking breast cancer and hantavirus infection. Despite the severe pathogenicity associated with hantavirus infections, currently available antiviral therapies remain limited, emphasizing the continuing need to identify new antiviral scaffolds for future investigation [14]. In the present work, we report the synthesis and computational evaluation of a novel nitrothiophene- derived Schiff base ligand (N1). The primary objective of this study was to investigate its interaction with multiple breast cancer-associated kinase targets, including EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K, which collectively regulate tumor proliferation, survival, and angiogenesis. As an exploratory extension of this computational investigation, the ligand was also docked against the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein to assess whether this chemical scaffold exhibits potential binding capability toward a structurally unrelated viral protein involved in RNA encapsidation. This exploratory comparison should not be interpreted as evidence of a unified therapeutic strategy but rather as an initial computational assessment of the molecular recognition properties of N1 across biologically distinct protein targets. The ligand (N1E,N8E)-N1,N8-bis((5- nitrothiophen-2-yl)methylene)naphthalene-1,8-diamine, and its in silico activities are reported here for the first time. Figure 1. The figure illustrates the proposed mechanism of action of the investigated ligand against major breast cancer-associated signaling proteins, including EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K. Activation of EGFR and HER2 normally initiates downstream signaling cascades such as the RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK and PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathways, which promote cancer cell proliferation, survival, and metastasis. VEGFR2 activation stimulates angiogenic signaling pathways responsible for tumor vascularization and endothelial cell migration. In the proposed mechanism, inhibition of these receptors suppresses phosphorylation-mediated signaling events, thereby reducing tumor growth, angiogenesis, and metastatic progression. PI3K inhibition further decreases AKT/mTOR signaling, leading to apoptosis induction and suppression of cancer cell survival. Overall, the figure demonstrates the multi-target inhibitory action of the ligand against critical pathways involved in breast cancer progression Journal of Polymer and Biopolymer Physics Chemistry 3 Figure 2. The figure represents the life cycle of Andes hantavirus and the proposed antiviral mechanism of the investigated compound targeting the viral nucleoprotein (N protein). The hantavirus initially enters the host cell through receptor-mediated endocytosis, followed by viral uncoating and release of ribonucleoprotein complexes into the cytoplasm. Viral RNA transcription and replication are subsequently carried out by the viral RNA- dependent RNA polymerase, leading to synthesis of viral proteins and assembly of new virions. The proposed ligand is suggested to bind within the RNA-binding region of the hantavirus nucleoprotein, thereby interfering with viral RNA encapsidation and ribonucleoprotein complex formation. This inhibition may suppress viral replication, reduce formation of mature viral particles, and prevent further viral dissemination within host cells. The overall antiviral outcome includes inhibition of viral replication, reduction of viral load, and prevention of hantavirus propagation 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Synthesis: Material All starting materials and solvents used were purchased from Aldrich and Fluka and were used without further purification. Melting points were determined in an open capillary tube on a Gallenkamp (Variable heater) melting point apparatus. NMR spectrum (1H) was recorded on an analysis X-685 benchtop NMR spectrophotometer at 60 MHz DMSO-d6 with TMS as internal standard, at the central science laboratory, Covenant University, Ota. The infrared spectra of all synthesized products were obtained using Agilent Cary 630 FTIR. The electronic spectra, of all the compounds, were obtained in solution, in the wavelength range 400-1000 nm using 1800 Shimadzu ultra-violet spectrophotometer. Both were carried out at the central science laboratory, Obafemi Awolowo University, Ile-Ife. 2.2. Synthesis; Experimental An ethanolic solution of 1,8-diaminonaphthalene (0.83 g, 5.00 mmol) was introduced to a solution of 5-nitro-2- carboxaldehyde (1.62 g, 10.0 mmol) in absolute ethanol (25 mL) supplemented with glacial acetic acid (3 drops) as a catalyst. The reaction mixture was subjected to reflux conditions for 4 hours under atmospheric pressure. Following thermal treatment, the reaction vessel was allowed to equilibrate to ambient temperature, after which the volatile organic solvent was removed via rotary evaporation under reduced pressure until precipitation of a solid product occurred. The crude material was subsequently triturated with cold ethanol and subjected to recrystallization from a chloroform/ethanol solvent mixture (volume ratio 30:70). A deep orange-colored solid was obtained, collected by vacuum filtration, and dried under reduced pressure at 60°C until constant mass was achieved, yielding N1 as the isolated product. The compound demonstrated appreciable solubility in chloroform, ethanol, and methanol. The schematic representation for the preparation of N1 is given in Scheme 1. Yield: 1.49 g, 68.78%; m.p: 165 ̊C - 166 ̊C (d); IR (cm−1): 1608 ν(C=C), 1587 ν(C=N), 1423 ν(C=C, thiophene aromatic ring) 1490 and 1326 ν(NO2), UV-Vis (nm): 299; 1 H NMR (60 MHz): DMSO-d6 δ 7.95 (s, 1H), 7.21, 7.04 (d, 6H), 6.64, 6.55 (d, 2H). Scheme 1. Schematic representation of the synthesis pathway of the novel Schiff base ligand N1, (N1E,N8E)-N1,N8-bis((5-nitrothiophen-2- yl)methylene)naphthalene-1,8-diamine formed through the condensation reaction between 5-nitrothiophene-2-carbaldehyde and naphthalene-1,8- diamine. The figure also illustrates the optimized three-dimensional molecular structure of the synthesized compound 2.3. Retrieval of Protein Structures The three-dimensional crystal structures of the selected 4 Journal of Polymer and Biopolymer Physics Chemistry therapeutic targets associated with breast cancer and viral infection were retrieved from the Protein Data Bank (PDB). The protein structures used in this study included epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR, PDB ID: 1M17, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2, PDB ID: 3PP0), vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 (VEGFR2, PDB ID: 1YWN), phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K, PDB ID: 4JPS), and Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein (PDB ID: 5E04 ). The biologically relevant protein chain (Chain A) was selected for all docking studies. These structures were chosen based on their high crystallographic resolution and the presence of co- crystallized ligands within the active site, allowing accurate definition of the ligand-binding pocket for molecular docking. 2.4. Protein Preparation Protein preparation was performed using AutoDock Tools. Prior to docking, all crystallographic water molecules, co-crystallized ligands, and non-essential heteroatoms were removed while preserving the protein backbone and active-site residues. Polar hydrogen atoms were subsequently added, and Kollman united-atom partial charges were assigned to the protein structures. The prepared receptors were saved in PDBQT format for docking calculations [19]. 2.5. Ligand Preparation The chemical structure of the synthesized ligand was generated using ChemDraw Professional 12.0 and converted into a three-dimensional structure using Avogadro . Geometry optimization was carried out using the MMFF94 force field until convergence to obtain a minimum-energy conformation. Hydrogen atoms were added, appropriate protonation corresponding to physiological pH (approximately 7.4) was assigned, and Gasteiger partial atomic charges were calculated using AutoDock Tools. The optimized ligand was finally converted into PDBQT format for molecular docking [20,21]. 2.6. Molecular Docking Molecular docking studies were performed using AutoDock Vina (version 1.2.7) to evaluate the binding affinity and binding mode of the ligand against the selected protein targets. The docking grid was centered on the active-site region defined by the co-crystallized ligand in each receptor structure. A grid box of 25 × 25 × 25 Å with a grid spacing of 1.0 Å was employed to adequately encompass the entire binding pocket. Docking calculations were carried out using an exhaustiveness value of 8, and 10 binding poses were generated for each protein-ligand complex. The resulting docking conformations were ranked according to their predicted binding free energies (kcal/mol). The optimal binding pose for each complex was selected based on the lowest binding free energy together with a favorable binding orientation and the formation of key interactions with biologically relevant active-site residues identified from the corresponding crystal structures and supported by previous literature [22,23]. 2.7. Drug-Likeness Evaluation The drug-likeness properties of N1 were evaluated using widely accepted computational pharmacokinetic filters, including Lipinski’s Rule of Five and Ghose’s filter, to assess its suitability as a potential orally active therapeutic agent. Physicochemical parameters such as molecular weight, hydrogen bond acceptors, hydrogen bond donors, partition coefficient (logP), molar refractivity, and total number of atoms were calculated to determine the drug-like behavior and oral bioavailability of the compound [24,25]. Lipinski’s Rule of Five was applied based on the criteria of molecular weight below 500 Da, hydrogen bond acceptors fewer than 10, hydrogen bond donors fewer than 5, and logP value below 5, which are considered favorable for oral drug candidates [24]. In addition, Ghose’s filter was employed to further evaluate the compound by considering acceptable ranges of molecular weight, lipophilicity, molar refractivity, and atom count commonly associated with biologically active molecules [25]. All calculations and predictions were performed using an online ADMET and drug-likeness prediction platform. The obtained parameters were analyzed to determine the compliance of N1 with established drug- likeness criteria 2.8. full_text_sections.full_text: Journal of Polymer and Biopolymer Physics Chemistry, 2026, Vol. 14, No. 1, 1-14 Available online at http://pubs.sciepub.com/jpbpc/14/1/1 Published by Science and Education Publishing DOI:10.12691/jpbpc-14-1-1 Computational Evaluation of a Novel Nitrothiophene- Derived Schiff Base Ligand Against Breast Cancer-Associated Proteins and Andes Hantavirus Nucleoprotein: Molecular Docking and ADMET Analysis Temitayo O. Aiyelabola1,*, Sayantan Pradhan2,*, Takashiro Akitsu3 1Department of Chemistry, Faculty of Science, Obafemi Awolowo University, Ile-Ife, Osun State, Nigeria 2Chemical Science Division, Saha Institute of Nuclear Physics, Kolkata, West Bengal, India 3Department of Chemistry, Faculty of Science, Tokyo University of Science, 1-3 Kagurazaka, Shinjuku-ku, Tokyo 162-8601, Japan *Corresponding author: Received August 10, 2026; Revised September 19, 2026; Accepted September 25, 2026 Abstract The identification of small molecules capable of interacting with multiple therapeutically relevant protein targets is an important strategy in early-stage drug discovery. In the present study, the Schiff base ligand ((N1E,N8E)-N1,N8-bis((5-nitrothiophen-2-yl)methylene)naphthalene-1,8-diamine; N1) was computationally evaluated against a panel of representative disease-associated proteins to investigate its target-binding profile. The primary focus was the assessment of N1 against breast cancer-associated receptor kinases, including EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K, which play central roles in oncogenic signaling pathways. In addition, the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein was included as an exploratory antiviral target to examine the broader target recognition capability of the ligand rather than to propose a common therapeutic mechanism. Molecular docking studies were performed using AutoDock Vina with experimentally determined protein structures obtained from the Protein Data Bank. N1 demonstrated favorable binding affinities toward all investigated breast cancer targets, with docking scores of −8.708 kcal/mol for EGFR, −8.836 kcal/mol for HER2, −8.906 kcal/mol for VEGFR2, and −9.066 kcal/mol for PI3K. The ligand also exhibited a docking score of −8.8 kcal/mol against the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein. Interaction analysis revealed multiple stabilizing hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic contacts, electrostatic interactions, and π-mediated interactions within the respective binding pockets.Drug-likeness assessment indicated compliance with Lipinski's and Ghose's rules, while ADMET prediction suggested favorable absorption and membrane permeability. Nevertheless, the predicted risks of hepatotoxicity, cardiotoxicity, and mutagenicity indicate that further structural optimization and experimental validation are required. Overall, this study demonstrates the potential of N1 as a promising scaffold for breast cancer-associated kinase inhibition while providing preliminary evidence of its broader protein-binding capability across biologically distinct targets. Keywords: Breast cancer, Hantavirus, Molecular docking, Drug-likeness, ADMET, Schiff base Cite This Article: Temitayo O. Aiyelabola, Sayantan Pradhan, and Takashiro Akitsu, “Computational Evaluation of a Novel Nitrothiophene-Derived Schiff Base Ligand Against Breast Cancer-Associated Proteins and Andes Hantavirus Nucleoprotein: Molecular Docking and ADMET Analysis.” Journal of Polymer and Biopolymer Physics Chemistry, vol. 14, no. 1 (2026): 1-14. doi: 10.12691/jpbpc-14-1-1. 1. Introduction Cancer and viral infections remain among the most serious global health challenges due to their high mortality rates, rapid disease progression, and limited availability of effective therapeutic agents [1,2]. Among different malignancies, breast cancer is one of the most frequently diagnosed cancers and represents a leading cause of cancer-related death among women worldwide [3]. The development and progression of breast cancer are closely associated with abnormal activation of receptor tyrosine kinases and intracellular signaling proteins, particularly Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR), Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2 (HER2), Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor Receptor 2 (VEGFR2), and phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) [4,5,6]. These signaling proteins regulate essential cellular processes such as proliferation, angiogenesis, migration, metastasis, survival, and apoptosis. Overexpression or mutation of these targets has been strongly linked with aggressive tumor 2 Journal of Polymer and Biopolymer Physics Chemistry progression and poor clinical prognosis [7]. EGFR and HER2 activation initiates downstream signaling cascades, including the RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK and PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathways, which contribute to uncontrolled cancer cell proliferation, enhanced survival, and metastatic progression (Figure 1) [8,9]. VEGFR2 plays a crucial role in tumor angiogenesis by stimulating endothelial cell migration and vascular formation necessary for tumor growth and metastasis [10]. PI3K, a central component of the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway, regulates cellular growth, proliferation, metabolism, and survival and is frequently dysregulated in breast cancer [11]. Collectively, EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K represent interconnected signaling proteins that regulate complementary aspects of breast cancer progression, including cell proliferation, survival, angiogenesis, and metastasis. Since these proteins belong to functionally linked oncogenic signaling networks, their simultaneous computational evaluation provides an opportunity to investigate whether a single chemical scaffold can potentially interact with multiple biologically relevant targets involved in breast cancer. It should be noted that the present study aims to explore the binding characteristics of N1 toward these proteins through molecular docking and does not imply experimentally validated inhibition of these signaling pathways. Therefore, EGFR, HER2, VEGFR2, and PI3K were selected as representative breast cancer-associated targets for an exploratory computational target-profiling study (Figure 1) [8,9,10,11]. In addition to cancer, viral infections caused by emerging and re-emerging viruses continue to pose major public health concerns worldwide. Andes hantavirus, a member of the Hantaviridae family, is responsible for hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), a severe respiratory disease associated with high fatality rates [12]. The viral nucleoprotein (N protein) plays an essential role in viral RNA encapsidation, ribonucleoprotein complex formation, genome replication, and viral assembly, making it a biologically relevant target for antiviral drug discovery (Figure 2) [13]. Unlike viral enzymes, the nucleoprotein does not possess catalytic activity; instead, its RNA-binding region is responsible for recognizing and stabilizing viral genomic RNA during ribonucleoprotein assembly. Accordingly, the molecular docking analysis in the present study focused on this functionally important RNA-binding region to evaluate the potential molecular recognition of N1. Binding at this site may theoretically interfere with RNA recognition or ribonucleoprotein assembly; however, such effects remain computational hypotheses that require experimental validation [13,14]. The inclusion of the Andes hantavirus nucleoprotein was intended as an exploratory assessment of the binding versatility of the N1 scaffold against a structurally unrelated viral target rather than to propose a unified therapeutic strategy linking breast cancer and hantavirus infection. Despite the severe pathogenicity associated with hantavirus infections, currently available antiviral therapies remain limited, emphasizing the continuing need to identify new antiviral scaffolds for future investigation [14]. In the present work, we report the synthesis and computational evaluation of a novel nitrothiophene- derived Schiff base ligand (N1). papers.title: From Systemic Inflammation to Calcium Leak: The RyR2 Hypothesis of Reversible Myocardial Dysfunction in Andes Virus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome
papers.abstract: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) caused by Andes virus is a severe zoonotic disease characterized by a paradoxical cardiac phenotype: profound myocardial dysfunction that is frequently reversible in survivors and occurs without extensive structural damage. The mechanisms linking systemic inflammation to this reversible dysfunction remain unknown. This review examines the hypothesis that inflammatory signaling converges on the cardiac ryanodine receptor (RyR2), a major intracellular Ca2+-release channel, through post-translational modifications, generating reversible myocardial dysfunction in HCPS. In severe disease, elevated IL-6, reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, and nitrosative stress activate pathways that in experimental models converge on RyR2 through CaMKII-dependent phosphorylation at Ser2814, oxidative modification of cysteine residues, and S-nitrosylation, each destabilizing the channel and promoting diastolic Ca2+ leak. The resulting increase in spontaneous Ca2+ release reduces SR Ca2+ content, impairs contractility, and predisposes to arrhythmias. This framework identifies RyR2 as a plausible mechanistic hub for the reversible cardiac phenotype. Therapeutic implications are discussed, emphasizing the timing of interventions and the potential of rycals, drugs that stabilize the closed state of RyR2 and prevent diastolic Ca2+ leak, as an emerging strategy. This model provides a testable hypothesis for a disease that currently lacks specific treatment.

source_records.abstract: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) caused by Andes virus is a severe zoonotic disease characterized by a paradoxical cardiac phenotype: profound myocardial dysfunction that is frequently reversible in survivors and occurs without extensive structural damage. The mechanisms linking systemic inflammation to this reversible dysfunction remain unknown. This review examines the hypothesis that inflammatory signaling converges on the cardiac ryanodine receptor (RyR2), a major intracellular Ca2+-release channel, through post-translational modifications, generating reversible myocardial dysfunction in HCPS. In severe disease, elevated IL-6, reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, and nitrosative stress activate pathways that in experimental models converge on RyR2 through CaMKII-dependent phosphorylation at Ser2814, oxidative modification of cysteine residues, and S-nitrosylation, each destabilizing the channel and promoting diastolic Ca2+ leak. The resulting increase in spontaneous Ca2+ release reduces SR Ca2+ content, impairs contractility, and predisposes to arrhythmias. This framework identifies RyR2 as a plausible mechanistic hub for the reversible cardiac phenotype. Therapeutic implications are discussed, emphasizing the timing of interventions and the potential of rycals, drugs that stabilize the closed state of RyR2 and prevent diastolic Ca2+ leak, as an emerging strategy. This model provides a testable hypothesis for a disease that currently lacks specific treatment.

papers.title: Hantaviral therapeutics: life cycle targets and chemotherapeutic interventions
papers.abstract: Orthohantaviruses represent a persistent global health threat, being responsible for life-threatening diseases such as Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) and Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS). Despite high case fatality rates and recent outbreaks, there are currently no universally licensed antivirals or vaccines. Clinical management remains heavily reliant on supportive care and repurposed drugs, which often exhibit limited efficacy and dose-limiting toxicities. This review examines rational drug design strategies targeting critical steps in the viral life cycle, specifically Gn/Gc-mediated cellular entry and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp)-driven genome replication. We evaluate the current landscape of viral inhibitors, including peptidomimetics, nucleoside analogues, and naturally derived compounds. To accelerate the discovery of novel treatments, we advocate for the integration of modern in silico screening to evaluate extensive chemical and natural product libraries. These broad compound collections offer a structurally diverse and largely untapped reservoir for antiviral development. Ultimately, expanding preclinical testing to include globally neglected variants will be essential to develop broad-spectrum hantaviral therapeutics capable of mitigating future epidemic threats.

KEYWORDS antiviral discovery, drug development, orthohantavirus, chemotherapeutics, phytochemicals, viral entry inhibitors, RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) inhibitors, viral life cycle targets Introduction The April 2026 Andes hantavirus outbreak on a cruise ship served as a reminder of the ongoing challenges pathogens pose to global public health (Andes Virus Outbreak Working Group, 2026; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2026; World Health Organization, 2026b). The high case fatality rate highlights that there are currently no universally licensed antivirals or vaccines against orthohantavirus infections (World Health Organization, 2026a). These rodent-borne pathogens belong to the family Hantaviridae, genus Orthohantavirus, and are enveloped, tri-segmented, single-stranded negative-sense RNA viruses (Jonsson et al., 2010). They cause two distinct, life-threatening clinical syndromes, one being Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) in Eurasia, and Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS) in the Americas (Heyman et al., 2009). Once internalized via endocytosis, a drop in endosomal pH forces the viral envelope to fuse with the host membrane, releasing the genome into the cytoplasm. The viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) starts both transcription and genome replication, before structural proteins and newly synthesized RNA assemble at the Golgi complex or plasma membrane prior to budding out as mature infectious virions (see Figure 1) (Hussein et al., 2011; Hepojoki et al., 2012; Vaheri et al., 2013b; Bradfute et al., 2024).
